140-the-jungle:
Lithuanian immigrants Jurgis and Ona arrive in Chicago hoping for work and a wedding. Upton Sinclair's Jungle, published in 1906, follows them into the stockyards, where packers grind men as they grind meat. Wages, housing, and graft crush the family step by step.

Sinclair details filth, accidents, and fraud in the packing plants with unsparing force. Jurgis turns to crime, politics, and finally socialism for an answer. The novel shocked readers and pushed food-safety reform. Its power as protest fiction has never faded. Sinclair's exposé led Congress toward the Pure Food and Drug Act within months.
15-moby-dick-or-the-whale:
A young sailor signs aboard a whaling ship and meets a captain consumed by one whale. Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, published in 1851, opens with Ishmael's restless call to the sea. The Pequod sails from Nantucket under Captain Ahab.

Chapters mix adventure with long essays on whales, whaling craft, and the sea. Ahab's hunt for the white whale drives crew and ship toward wreck. Queequeg, Starbuck, and Stubb give the voyage its human range. The novel's depth made it a central work of American letters. Later readers found in Ahab's hunt a study of obsession, nature, and the limits of knowledge.
171-charlotte-temple:
Charlotte Temple, a schoolgirl of fifteen, trusts a soldier's promises and elopes to America. Susanna Rowson's Charlotte Temple, once America's best-selling novel, follows her from a boarding school to New York. Her lover abandons her, and poverty, illness, and shame follow.

Rowson pauses the tale to warn young readers against seduction and false friends. A kind stranger and a dying mother's letter frame Charlotte's repentance. The novel's sentimentality moved generations of American readers to tears. Its grave in New York became a place of pilgrimage. Rowson's moral tale warned a young republic about seduction, and its lessons echoed for a century.
19669-twenty-years-of-balkan-tangle:
M. Edith Durham was a British traveler who knew the Balkans better than most outsiders. Twenty Years of Balkan Tangle grew from her journeys through the Near East. It opens with a sea trip among mauve islets in a dazzling blue sea. Strange tongues and stranger garments greeted her at each port. She writes that the fascination of the region took hold of her there.

Durham spent years among Albanians and their neighbors. She learned languages, recorded customs, and took sides in local causes. The Balkans of her years there were a knot of empires and new nations. Her book untangles that knot from ground level. It stays a key eyewitness source for the region.
19705-border-and-bastille:
Border and Bastille is a nineteenth-century memoir of travel and hardship. Its author thanks patrons who helped him reach the post he wanted. He admits one benefactor kindly overrated his qualifications. Such prefaces were the era's way of settling debts in print. The title joins a border crossing with a prison, the Bastille. Both promise trouble met on the road.

Memoirs of this kind fed a public hungry for foreign scenes. A border meant new laws, new tongues, and new risks. A prison meant the state showing its teeth. The author moves between gratitude and grievance in his opening. That mix often signals a life spent seeking favor abroad. The book belongs to the confessional travel shelf of its century.
19711-the-buried-temple:
Maurice Maeterlinck was a Belgian writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Buried Temple gathers his essays on moral and unseen forces. One passage asks whether an intelligent Judge must exist. It wonders whether cheating a neighbor cheats all the forces of justice too. Maeterlinck writes philosophy as quiet, searching prose.

His essays circle death, fate, silence, and the soul. The buried temple of the title is the hidden shrine within each person. Readers meet symbolist thought at its most gentle. Maeterlinck avoids system and proof on purpose. He prefers wonder that stays honest about mystery. The book is a calm entry into his meditative work.
19824-horses-nine-stories-of-harness-and:
Sewell Ford's Horses, from 1903, collects nine stories of harness and saddle. One hero, Skipper, joins the force at the age of six. He is clean of limb and sound of wind, without a blemish. A Green Mountain boy broke him to saddle. That boy knew more of horse nature than of trashy book learning. Ford's horses are working animals with full characters.

Ford wrote beloved animal stories set in New York and Vermont. His horses pull cabs, carry police, and haul loads. Each story tests the bond between horse and driver. The age of the horse was ending as he wrote. These tales preserve its skills and affections. Readers meet horsepower when it still had a heartbeat.
20054-the-mermaid-a-love-tale:
L. Dougall published The Mermaid, a love tale, in 1895. Its lead man, Caius Simpson, is the only son of a farmer. The farm lies on the north-west coast of Prince Edward's Island. His father worked hard, grew rich by island standards, and made his land yield well.

From that firm ground, a love story grows in a sea-bound place. Island farms, coasts, and small towns shape the lives on the page. The title hints at myth and the pull of the sea. Readers get romance rooted in work, land, and local custom.
20170-legend-land-vol-1-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume one, gathers old tales of the West of England. Years ago, a rich, lovely lady came at times to one church. No one knew where she came from or who she was. Her beauty and glorious voice set the whole parish talking of her.

Such mystery figures walk through many tales in this set. Old churches, moors, and coasts of the West Country frame them. The book saves tales told by word of mouth for print readers. Readers get ghosts, saints, and wonders from a land rich in legend.
20180-mr-kris-kringle-a-christmas-tale:
Mr. Kris Kringle is a Christmas tale named for Santa Claus himself. A touch of sadness dims the children's usual gay Christmas humor. That hopeful hour, so bright for the young, carries shadow here. Years bring such shadow to joy, the tale notes at its start.

Christmas tales of this era mix gifts with grief and grace. Poor children, kind strangers, and small miracles fill many such stories. The book aims to warm hearts while it tugs at them too. Readers get a tender holiday tale in the classic sentimental vein.
20214-instruction-for-using-a-slide-rule:
Instruction for Using a Slide Rule teaches a tool once vital to skilled work. Slide rules gave fast, close answers without long hand sums. Students, teachers, engineers, and architects all used them daily, it notes. Draftsmen, surveyors, and chemists found the rule just as handy at work.

Clerks and accountants used it when rough sums had to be rapid. The manual explains scales, settings, and worked examples step by step. Before electronic calculators, this slim tool ruled offices and labs. Readers get a clear fossil of practical math in the pre-digital age.
20249-legend-land-vol-2-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume two, gathers more old tales of the West of England. Brent Tor rises as a lone, church-crowned peak near Lydford. It stands like a sentry watching the West for grim Dartmoor. From afar, the brave little hill looks like a burst of flame.

Burnt Tor, they say, was its old name for just that reason. Saints, giants, and ghosts crowd the tales tied to such places. Each short piece ties a story to a tor, church, or moor. Readers get a second rich helping of West Country legend and lore.
20255-the-unruly-sprite-a-partial-fairy-:
Henry van Dyke wrote The Unruly Sprite, a partial fairy tale of visions and faith. Some beings in the tale seem as substantial as mountain mists. They flicker and stray like will-o'-the-wisps over dark, wet ground. Yet something immortal clings to them, the man in the tale knows.

Without their presence, the world would be nothing to him at all. Van Dyke blends fairy lore with gentle moral and spiritual counsel. His sprite stands for the wild, bright part of the soul. Readers get a short, lyrical tale from a beloved American essayist-preacher.
20314-pearl-and-periwinkle:
Pearl and Periwinkle is a children's tale of two orphans taken into a stiff home. The children are son and daughter of the family's outcast sister. She has been half-forgotten, though only two months dead, the book notes. Adopting her children strikes Miss Hetty as almost scandalous at first.

Worse still, the pair have traveled all their young lives with a circus. Circus ways clash with a prim household's rules and manners at once. Yet pathos softens that clash as the tale goes on. Young readers get a story of orphans, pride, and slowly opening hearts.
20328-simon-dale:
Anthony Hope wrote Simon Dale, a historical novel of Restoration England. It opens by praising a great man who left an enduring name. His rule for life was charity in mind, trust in providence. And truth as the pole on which a life should turn, it adds.

Simon Dale serves at the court of Charles the Second in this tale. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, loved courts and swordplay. Love, honor, and intrigue swirl around his young hero at Whitehall. Readers get polished historical romance from a master of the form.
20563-terry-a-tale-of-the-hill-people:
Charles Goff Thomson's Terry: A Tale of the Hill People opens with a shot in the winter hills. The frosty silence of the snow-covered hills is broken by the vicious crack of a high-powered, small-caliber rifle. A hidden hunter has fired from a thicket.

The hunter springs out and crosses the gully to a knoll. There lies a black furry bundle, the game he has brought down. Thomson builds his tale of the hill people on such scenes of hunting, hardship, and mountain custom. The hills themselves, white and silent, shape every life in the story.
20567-the-pigeon-tale:
Virginia Bennett's The Pigeon Tale is a story for children set in an old farmhouse that seems to wake up and dress itself young again. The fresh muslin curtains at the window are stiff with starch. They will not stir an inch in the breeze blowing in.

The old farmhouse, the narrator decides, is trying to look young again. To look young again: how many others wish the same. Into that brightened house comes the pigeon's tale, told in Bennett's gentle farm language. The book belongs to the shelf of quiet animal and farm stories written for young readers.
20580-napoleon-the-little:
Victor Hugo wrote Napoleon the Little as a furious attack on Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte after his coup of December 1851. Hugo, driven into exile, refused to call the new ruler Napoleon the Great's equal. This 1909 edition brought the polemic to English readers in a fresh form.

Its pages stage scenes from the fall of the republic. The representatives crowd the right lobby of the Assembly and return to their places, leaving the passage free. It was about four in the afternoon, and darkness was falling on the great hall. Hugo turns such scenes into an indictment of tyranny.
20709-from-pole-to-pole-a-book-for-young:
Sven Hedin, the Swedish explorer of Central Asia, wrote From Pole to Pole as a book of world travel for young people. Rather than tell his own expeditions, he takes readers on one great journey around the earth. Lands, peoples, and natural wonders pass in order along the route.

Our journey begins at Stockholm, the capital of my native country, he writes. Leaving Stockholm by train in the evening, we travel all night in comfortable sleeping cars. We arrive next morning at Trelleborg, Sweden's southernmost port, where the journey by sea begins. School readers across Europe learned geography from Hedin's ride.
20711-daily-thoughts-selected-from-the-w:
Daily Thoughts gathers short passages from the writings of Charles Kingsley, chosen for one day at a time. Kingsley was a clergyman, novelist, and naturalist whose sermons and books filled Victorian homes. A daily reading book lets his voice speak briefly each morning.

Kingsley urges readers to understand where we are, and what our work is here. He scorns superstitions about the good old times. Men fancy those days belonged to God, he says, while this age belongs only to man, blind chance, and the evil one. The selections mix devotion, nature, and social duty in his hearty style.
20716-the-tale-of-timothy-turtle:
Arthur Scott Bailey's The Tale of Timothy Turtle belongs to his Sleepy-Time Tales of the animals of Pleasant Valley. Timothy Turtle is an old, grumpy resident of Black Creek. All the wild folk know him by name, though few see much of him.

He is seen less often than Mr. Crow because he spends much of his time on the muddy bottom of Black Creek. Besides, he never flapped his way through the air to Farmer Green's fields. Bailey's animal tales taught children the habits of real creatures while dressing them in waistcoats of story.
20808-three-people:
A baby fresh from the bath, all curls and blue eyes, opens Three People. Isabella Alden, who wrote as Pansy, asks what such a child could be but a beauty. Hands, feet, and a rosebud mouth all quiver with life and glee.

Pansy wrote Christian tales for vast numbers of young readers. Three People weaves faith into home life and the growth of its leads. Her books taught conduct through story rather than sermon. This one keeps her warm tone and clear moral aim. It shows why her tales filled Sunday school shelves and family bookcases across America for decades.
20878-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-essay-:
Thomas Carlyle's works, says John Morley, form a canon closed and set for posterity. Thirty fine volumes hold his Gospel of Silence in compressed form. Morley's essay on Carlyle, in Critical Miscellanies, weighs that vast, strange legacy.

Carlyle thundered against his age as prophet, historian, and sage of Chelsea. Morley sorts his power from his faults with cool, clear judgment. Hero worship, German thought, and French revolt all fed Carlyle's fire. This essay gives new readers a firm guide into a writer who awed and irked his century in near equal parts.
20923-a-negro-explorer-at-the-north-pole:
Word that Matt Henson stood with Peary at the North Pole reached New York in 1909, this book recalls. A Peary Arctic Club man swore Henson must have been there that day. A Negro Explorer at the North Pole, from 1912, tells Henson's own tale.

Henson, a Black explorer of rare skill, drove dogs and broke trail for Peary. Cold, hunger, and ice perils fill his plain, strong account. White fame long slighted his share in the feat. His book claims that share with calm proof, and it remains a key voice from the heroic age of polar travel.
20939-the-song-of-the-exile:
England's shores shrink astern as The Song of the Exile opens in verse of parting pain. The singer owns he has little cause to mourn, for home gave him only unrest. Birth, yes, his native land gave, but never a true home.

Visions and miscellaneous poems fill the rest of this slight volume's pages. Exile, faith, loss, and hope sound through its gathered pieces in turn. Such verse spoke to many in an age of wide migration and parting. Readers meet a voice that turns private sorrow into song, plain in feeling even when its dress is old and formal.
21105-teddy-the-story-of-a-little-pickle:
John Conran Hutcheson wrote this short children's book about Teddy. The small boy's loud demand for his grandmother startles a railway porter out of his skin. Teddy is an independent young gentleman of about ten or eleven in spirit, forever in minor trouble. His small misdeeds fill most of the chapters.

The porter who first meets him is a tall, good-natured giant in worn velveteen clothes smeared with oil and grease. Hutcheson, better known for sea tales, keeps this story on land and at child height. It aims at young readers who enjoy seeing a pickle of a boy get into and out of scrapes.
21129-the-heart-of-una-sackville:
Una Sackville starts a diary in May 1895, in a handsome book with a clasp and key given her by Lena Streatham. Mrs George de Horne Vaizey tells Una's story through that diary, begun just as she leaves school. Una means to write only when she wants to talk and her friend Lorna is not near.

The tale follows a young woman of the professional middle classes. She looks for love and a husband in the months and years after school. Vaizey draws the men and women around Una sharply. Written close to its 1895 setting, it records the social world of such girls from inside.
21203-the-tale-of-grandfather-mole:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales introduce a queer old person who has lived in Farmer Green's garden longer than anyone can say. Neighbours seldom saw Grandfather Mole, since moles spend their lives underground. The frontispiece shows him making a rush at Mr. Meadow Mouse.

Bailey wrote a whole shelf of these animal tales, from Cuffy Bear to Dickie Deer Mouse, for Grosset and Dunlap. Each gives one creature a small comedy of habits, appetites, and quarrels with the neighbours. Grandfather Mole's grumbling ways underground make him a funny, cross old character for children hearing the stories at bedtime.
21272-the-bibliotaph-and-other-people:
Leon H. Vincent's essays on book lovers appeared in Boston in 1899, several of them first printed in the Atlantic Monthly. The Bibliotaph, his opening portrait, is a book collector buried in his books, drawn not wholly from imagination. Two more papers follow the same figure among his friends, scrapbooks, and bargain bins.

Other essays read the letters of John Keats and consider Thomas Hardy and an Elizabethan novelist. A third takes up Stevenson as vagabond and philosopher, ending with his novel St Ives. Vincent pokes gentle fun at collectors while sharing their passion. The volume preserves the talk of 1890s book rooms, where bargains and editions were serious sport.
21296-mother-carey-s-chicken-her-voyage-:
Mark Strong has always longed to follow his sea-captain father to sea. At last his father agrees to take both Mark and his mother on the next voyage. George Manville Fenn warns the boy that a man's duty is to face danger. A woman, he says, keeps the nest. But the family sails together anyway. The Java Seas await them.

Pirates, sharks, serpents, volcanoes, hostile peoples, geysers, and fire at sea crowd the voyage to the unknown isle of the title. Fenn piles peril on peril in his practised way. Mother Carey's chicken, a storm petrel, gives the tale its name and its sea flavour.
21314-king-o-the-beach-a-tropic-tale:
Carey, a teenage boy, sails on the steamer Chusan to join his parents in Australia in George Manville Fenn's tropic tale. He befriends the ship's doctor and seaman Bob Bostock. Then he falls from the rigging and is knocked out, his telescope taking the worst of the fall. A gale then drives the powerless ship onto a coral-girt volcanic island.

Most passengers escape by boat, but Carey is too hurt to move, so the doctor and Bostock stay with him on the wreck. A beachcomber who calls himself king of the islands arrives with a retinue and proves vicious. When he shoots the doctor, the tale turns toward rescue.
21333-doom-castle:
Neil Munro's novel of Jacobite Scotland opens on an autumn afternoon with wintry breakers sounding and nuts dropping in the corries of Ardkinglas. Count Victor, a foreigner, comes to a strange country and is pursued almost at once. The Baron of Doom and his castle give the tale its centre.

Chapters promise a spy wanted, an apparition, a lawyer's good lady, and a woman at a window. Mungo Boyd and chamberlain Sim MacTaggart serve the household as intrigue gathers. A duel on the sands, a cell in the fosse, and the Duke's ball carry the action. Munro, a Highland writer, sets romance and conspiracy in the Argyll he knew well.
21344-the-young-bridge-tender-or-ralph-n:
Arthur M. Winfield, who also wrote the Rover Boys books, opens with Ralph Nelson, only son of a widow. His father once kept the swing bridge between Westville and Eastport on Keniscot Lake. Ralph holds the bridge tender's job himself when a smash at the bridge starts the action. Squire Paget wants the property and moves against the family.

Chapters follow a missing bill, a runaway, a midnight crime, and Ralph out on bail before the robbery is cleared up. Percy, the squire's son, hears something that matters. Winfield wrote upward-struggle tales for boys in the Alger line: honest work, false suspicion, and a rise earned by pluck.
21449-with-axe-and-rifle:
A boy watches his Irish family make a home in the wild West in W. H. G. Kingston's With Axe and Rifle. His father liked the country so well that he went back to Ireland for his bride. The boy, his brother Dan, and small sister Kathleen grow up on the frontier.

Kingston shows the settlers' grind against weather, sickness, bad neighbours, and raids. A tutor called the Dominie and Dio, a runaway slave they shelter, stand close to the family. A wicked man named Bracher and a strange hunter who keeps saving them add drama. The tale ends in sudden, glad relief.
21577-peter-simple:
Peter Simple is the fool of his family, and the navy gets him, in Captain Marryat's novel of 1834. His father, a clergyman and a noble family's youngest son, holds a rich living. Custom, Peter jokes, offers the family's greatest fool to the country's naval greatness.

At fourteen Peter is packed off, first to a stockbroker and then to sea. His slow wits prove sharper than folk think, as cruises and captures pile up. The book was Marryat's fourth, and it fixed his fame for comic sea fiction. Friendship with the loyal O'Brien gives the tale much of its heart.
21616-the-ape-the-idiot-other-people:
W. C. Morrow gathers dark tales in The Ape, the Idiot and Other People, copyrighted in 1897. The stories first ran in Lippincott's Magazine and in San Francisco papers. A fourth edition, from 1910, is the copy given here.

One tale opens on an ape who has lived in a cage since childhood, with no memory of free forests. Others treat a plague hero, a monster-maker, and a game of honour. Absinthe, dungeons, and faithful amulets supply the props of these grim pieces. Morrow writes with a cold, exact hand that made him a master of the weird tale.
21692-the-pirate-city-an-algerine-tale:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Pirate City in Algiers, in a tale of action about 1817. A dear little old lady in Sicily opens the tale, her mouth a study of smiles. Her wrinkles, Ballantyne says, are each a separate smile around it.

Her son Lucien is meant for the Church, by his father's dearest wish. Juliet, an adopted child, is promised to a convent by her uncle the abbot. Against those quiet plans stands the pirate city itself, and its defeat by the British Navy. Ballantyne mixes comic portraiture at home with Barbary fighting abroad.
21733-the-giant-of-the-north-pokings-rou:
Arctic seas call in this Ballantyne adventure, whose subtitle promises pokings round the Pole. Ballantyne had lived in the Canadian north as a young Hudson's Bay clerk, and ice country was his home ground as a writer. His tales of the far north drew on real cold, real hunger, and real travel by sledge and boat.

The giant of the title and the voyage toward the Pole drive the story's wonders. Strange sights, hard weather, and tall tales gather around the push into the frozen seas. Ballantyne mixes fact from polar travel with a boy's love of marvels. The result is a northern yarn in his fullest storyteller's voice, equal parts camp talk and adventure.
21837-monopolies-and-the-people:
Trusts and monopolies are put on trial in this 1889 study by Charles Whiting Baker, an editor of The Engineering News. Baker promises two things: a fair survey of monopolies in every industry, and a plain discussion of their causes, growth, evils, and remedies. He admits his list cannot name every powerful combination, yet holds that the broad facts deserve wide knowledge.

The book is dedicated to all who love truth, justice, and the rights of the whole people. It appeared as the great trusts were reshaping American business and politics. Baker writes as an engineer among lawyers: facts first, then judgment. For readers of the trust era, it is a clear contemporary map of the fight that led to antitrust law.
21975-the-barbadoes-girl-a-tale-for-youn:
An orphan girl from the West Indies joins an English family in Mrs. Hofland's The Barbadoes Girl, a tale for young people reissued at Boston in 1863. Mr. Harewood tells his wife and children that the daughter of a dead friend is coming from Barbados to live with them. The children pepper him with questions. Edmund is grave and studious at twelve, Charles lively at ten, and Ellen, eight, the mildest and most modest of all.

Bacon and Addison supply the mottoes: indulged passion makes bitter work for repentance. Hofland was a prolific writer of improving tales. Her new girl's temper and the family's patience drive the lesson home. The book teaches the management of feeling through a stranger in the house, in the firm Victorian manner.
22174-andrew-melville:
William Morison wrote this life of Andrew Melville for the Famous Scots series. Melville, scholar and church reformer, led Scotland's Presbyterians after Knox. The struggle from 1574 to 1688 to keep the Presbyterian system fills the book. Morison argues that the system's benefits to Scotland justify that struggle.

Melville defied kings, rebuilt universities, and suffered exile for the Kirk's freedom. His famous rebuke of James VI, calling him God's silly vassal, echoes through the story. Morison writes in the brisk, admiring style of the Famous Scots volumes. The book gives general readers a compact life of the second founder of Scottish Presbyterianism.
22185-sonnie-boy-s-people:
James B. Connolly, the Irish-American writer of sea stories, published Sonnie-Boy's People as a set of tales. Connolly knew Gloucester fishermen and harbour towns at first hand. In the title story, Marie Welkie watches a stranger from her veranda while keeping an eye on her nephew. His fine clothes and easy assurance disturb and amuse her; his kindness to the boy pleases her more.

The stories circle Sonnie-Boy, a child among sailors, fishermen, and shore folk. Connolly writes dialect and sea talk with a reporter's ear. Humour and pathos mix in his port scenes. The collection shows why Connolly was rated among the best American sea-story writers of his day.
22264-irish-books-and-irish-people:
Stephen Gwynn wrote Irish Books and Irish People as essays on his country's letters and life. Behind everything, Gwynn says, lies a great social change. Ownership of Ireland's land was passing from landlords to the men who tilled it. That transfer, he argues, literally unenslaved three-fourths of Ireland's people, though its links to the life of the mind are obscure and intangible.

His essays connect the land change to Ireland's literary revival. Books, writers, and readers all stand in the new Ireland's making. Gwynn, a nationalist member of Parliament and man of letters, writes as an insider. The volume captures the Irish revival's confidence in the years before the Great War.
22346-exile:
Exile is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its figures belong to a strange order of scholars in robes. One of them, Oktan, stands slightly under Kinton's height of five feet ten.

Oktan has a long, supple trunk and short, bowed legs. His short, thick arms are carried high before his chest. That build leaves Kinton feeling something is out of proportion. Robes hide part of the oddness from casual eyes. Such close body detail builds an alien presence without explanation. Readers meet exiles whose forms set them apart. The tale plays on difference, strangeness, and the unease of standing near it.
22399-the-fireside-picture-alphabet-or-h:
The Fireside Picture Alphabet mixes an alphabet book with humor and droll moral tales. Its back pages advertise the publisher's other wares for children. Miss Hattie's French Bedstead and Tom Thumb's Carriage appear there.

New toys in preparation are also promised to young buyers. A manual of cricket and baseball is offered by mail. Its plans show how to lay out grounds and form clubs. Marylebone Club rules for cricket are included in that manual. Baseball rules from several clubs appear alongside them. As a whole, the volume shows how children's books were sold. Pictures taught letters while advertisements sold the next purchase.
22763-suite-mentale:
Randall Garrett wrote Suite Mentale, a science fiction story about minds joined in a telepathic gestalt and the strain of sharing thoughts. The catalog record gives no year. Garrett, a prolific magazine writer, liked clever premises worked out with a light, ironic hand, and a mental suite, minds in sequence like music, is one of his neatest.

The sample is pure Garrett misdirection. A doctor gives his brief verdict, he may live. His audience is a group of men in conservative business suits, holding soft felt hats outside the door. Mallon's eyes stop on the tallest man's face. Nothing in the scene admits how strange the case behind the door has been. The story that follows thinks hard about what linked minds would do to privacy, guilt, and selfhood.
22827-patchwork-a-story-of-the-plain-peo:
Anna Balmer Myers set Patchwork, her 1920 story of the Plain People, among Pennsylvania's plain-dressing farm families. A perfect June morning opens the tale, with perfume from countless blossoms tempting everyone outdoors. Sunshine, blue sky, and lavish early summer set the scene before any conflict arrives.

Against that beauty, Myers works out the tensions of a strict, close community. Young people in plain dress face the pull of the wider world, its clothes, music, and freedoms. The patchwork of the title fits both the quilts of the region and the pieced-together lives on the page. Myers knew this world well, and her sympathy shows. The novel remains a warm, informed portrait of Pennsylvania Dutch country life.
22948-rival-pitchers-of-oakdale:
Morgan Scott opens Rival Pitchers of Oakdale, published in 1911, at noon on a sunny April day. Boys cluster on the Oakdale Academy steps at noon, talking nothing but baseball. The season is about to open, and Scott says the fever of the game already runs in their veins.

Two pitchers, one mound. The rivalry promised by the title drives this entry in Scott's Oakdale sports series, with school honor and a girl's opinion never far away. The books sold clean competition to boy readers, complete with coaching in both pitching and conduct. Period slang and period certainty fill the pages. As a record of how America taught sport to its sons, it is hard to beat.
23126-eric-or-little-by-little:
A boy counts the days in Eric, or Little by Little. A young boy capers and claps at the news. His parents come home within the week, the family will stay a short while, and then, at last, school begins for him.

Frederic William Farrar's school story follows Eric Williams through an English public school, where small surrenders to temptation accumulate, little by little, into ruin. Few Victorian novels were pressed on schoolboys so hard, or remembered so vividly, fondly and ruefully at once. Farrar, a clergyman and schoolmaster, wrote to warn, and his warning became a genre landmark. Modern readers meet the original of a hundred school stories, sermon and all, with its pathos fully intact.
23148-droozle:
A puppy snake stars in Droozle. The narrator traces Droozle to art school days and a grand tour. An unscheduled stop in the Coffin system introduced him to ballpoint snakes, Coffin Two's chief export. By liftoff, one small snake had become his traveling companion.

A pet from another planet, carried home in a traveler's luggage, gives the story its gentle engine. Art school, a grand tour, and interstellar stopovers blend in a future where tourism includes other worlds. Droozle himself, part souvenir and part companion, tests what his owner owes a creature bought as a curiosity. The tone stays light, the questions real. It is a small, fond piece of science fiction about pets and responsibility.
459-the-white-people:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells a strange, quiet tale of a girl at a remote Scots castle in this short novel. The narrator, raised at Muircarrie among few kin, senses from childhood that she differs from other children. Visions and voices from beyond the veil visit her, bringing comfort rather than fear.

Burnett writes in a soft, first-person voice, letting mystery unfold without shock. The white people of the title are the dead, seen as near and kind. The book reads as a tender ghost story, more about love and loss than horror, and about a girl who learns that death may not end care.
501-the-story-of-doctor-dolittle:
Hugh Lofting tells of Doctor Dolittle, a Puddleby physician who learns animal speech, in this 1920 children's classic. When patients leave and debts grow, Dolittle turns to animal doctoring, with Polynesia the parrot as teacher. A message from Africa sends him, with his beasts, across the sea to cure sick monkeys.

Lofting writes and draws the voyage with gentle humor: a bridge of apes, a lion leader, and a rare pushmi-pullyu. Home again, Dolittle keeps his strange, kind practice. The book endures as a tale of a man who listens to beasts, and of a world where care crosses every species line.
506-the-shuttle:
Frances Hodgson Burnett weaves an Atlantic tale of two sisters and two houses in this novel. Bettina Vanderpoel, a rich American girl, crosses to England to rescue her sister Rosalie from a cruel earl at Stornham. The shuttle of the title shuttles wealth, love, and fate between New York and an old English village.

Burnett writes with rich detail, from Bond Street shops to marsh lanes. A young lord, a plain American, and a village full of watchers shape the plot. The novel charms as a transatlantic romance where a strong sister's will mends what rank and money broke.
523-court-life-in-china-the-capital-its-:
Isaac Taylor Headland, a professor at Peking University, describes late imperial China from inside the court in this study. His wife, physician to the Empress Dowager's kin, opened doors shut for years, letting him sketch the Forbidden City, its ladies, princes, and officials. Reform, the Boxer rising, and new schools frame the tale.

Chapters follow the Empress Dowager as girl, ruler, reactionary, reformer, artist, and woman, then turn to Emperor Kuang Hsu as prisoner and reformer. Headland argues the Dowager was misjudged by the West. The book serves as a rare firsthand portrait of a court on the edge of fall.
559-greenmantle:
John Buchan sends Richard Hannay on a Great War mission to the East in this spy thriller, sequel to The Thirty-Nine Steps. Hannay, Sandy, and Peter Pienaar must stop a German plot to raise a holy war with a prophet called Greenmantle. Disguised Dutchmen, caravanserais, and garden houses in Constantinople mark the road.

Buchan writes with brisk, boyish vigor, praising the war's strange truths over romance. His preface owns the tale was scribbled in odd moments. The novel endures as a classic of wartime adventure, where a few bold men play for empires with bluff and nerve.
751-the-autocrat-of-the-breakfast-table:
Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote this series of talks by the Autocrat, a witty Boston gentleman who holds forth at a boarding-house breakfast table. He discourses on books, science, human nature, and city life, while the other boarders chime in, tease, and tell their own tales. The talk ranges wide and never stays dull.

Holmes mixes essay, poem, and anecdote, with humour that is warm rather than biting. The Autocrat's table became a beloved fixture of American letters, and the book made Holmes famous. It still reads as a model of the familiar essay: learned, funny, and humane, in the voice of a man who loves talk for its own sake.
782-the-travels-of-sir-john-mandeville:
A traveller calling himself Sir John Mandeville told this famous account of the East in the fourteenth century, in the Cotton manuscript version here given in modern spelling. He claims to have journeyed to Jerusalem, Egypt, India, and Cathay, describing holy sites, strange beasts, and peoples of every custom.

Much of the book borrows from other writers, and its marvels, from dog-headed men to rivers of gems, are fables rather than facts. Yet it shaped how Europe imagined Asia for two hundred years. The volume, with three tales from Hakluyt added, is a key text of medieval travel lore, valued for its wonder and its influence.
944-the-voyage-of-the-beagle:
Charles Darwin wrote this journal of his voyage round the world aboard HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836. He states in his preface that the work grew from his notes on the voyage and from the zoology of the expedition. He tells of lands from South America to Australia and the Galápagos Isles.

Darwin describes animals, plants, rocks, and peoples with a naturalist's keen eye, noting finches, fossils, and earthquakes as he goes. The voyage shaped the theory he would later publish, and the journal shows that theory forming. The book remains a classic of travel and science, vivid, curious, and full of wonder.
a-dog-s-tale:
Mark Twain lets a dog tell her own story, beginning with her parentage: her father was a St. Bernard, her mother a collie, but she is a Presbyterian, as her mother told her. The mother, who picked up grand words at the dining-room door and Sunday school, taught her pup the uses of fine language. The family serves a kind master and his children.

Three chapters carry the dog from puppyhood to motherhood, through a fire she helps fight and a nursery she guards. Then human cruelty, dressed as science, strikes her own pup, and her loyalty meets a world that does not deserve it. Twain wrote the tale against cruelty to animals, and its plain pathos still lands.
a-girl-of-the-people:
A Girl of the People, by L T Meade, opens in a street crowd tugging at one girl's resolve. Meade's Bet stands stolid and straight while her companions chant that she is funking it, afraid to join their outing where Joe Wilkins, Sam, Jimmy, and Hester Wright wait round the corner. A dancing newspaper girl shakes a dirty hand in her face and calls her a mammy's girl, tied to her mother's apron strings, while the whole group laughs.

Bet flushes, pales, bites her lips, and answers with money instead of surrender: she tosses her share, a shilling, onto the pavement and marches home. That refusal sets the novel's terms. Meade follows a working class heroine. Her pleasures are real and her wages matter. Self respect costs her something every time she keeps it. Her friends spend theirs freely.
a-horse-s-tale:
Mark Twain tells a story in the voice of Soldier Boy, a horse who belongs to Buffalo Bill and serves with the army in the West. The title page of this edition, published in October 1907 with pictures by Lucius Hitchcock, shows the horse taken to an Indian camp. Soldier Boy is proud of his breeding and eager to explain horse society.

The tale mixes the horse's own chapters with letters from General Alison, his mother, and young Cathy, the girl Soldier Boy loves. Talk among horses, army life, a scout ride, and a bullfight scene fill the middle. Twain uses the animal's honest voice to mock human pride and cruelty.
a-jacobite-exile:
A Jacobite Exile is an 1894 adventure novel by G A Henty. Sir Marmaduke Carstairs is a Jacobite, a supporter of the exiled Stuart cause, and he is denounced as a plotter against King William. He and his son Charlie flee England for Sweden, where a very different war is being fought under King Charles the Twelfth.

Charlie joins the foreign legion in Swedish service and wins honor in several campaigns against the Poles and Russians. Henty folds the boy's exile into the great northern wars of the age, mixing real battles with a young soldier's rise. The novel gives readers both a Jacobite's grievance and a tour of Charles the Twelfth's battlefields.
a-modest-proposal-for-preventing-the-chi:
Jonathan Swift published his pamphlet in 1729, as its title page states, and it opens with a grim sight: beggar mothers in Ireland followed by ragged children with no food. The speaker then offers his modest proposal in the calm tone of a man of business. Poor parents, he says, should sell their infants as meat for rich tables.

He supports the plan with numbers, prices, and recipes, and lists its benefits for landlords, parents, and the kingdom. The horror builds because the voice never wavers or jokes. Swift meant the piece as an attack on English policy and cold economic thinking that treated Irish people as cattle.
a-prefect-s-uncle:
P. G. Wodehouse dates his school novel 1903 on the title page and opens as term begins at Beckford College, where Marriott hurls his portmanteau onto the senior day-room table. The contents promise an unusual uncle in chapter two, and the uncle making himself at home in chapter three. He is the Bishop, uncle to a prefect, and a cricketer of alarming energy.

Chapters follow the bishop's ride, the M.C.C. match, stump cricket and poetry, house matches, and a disputed authorship, through the winter term to the bishop scoring at last. Wodehouse, fresh from school himself, writes the world of houses, prefects, and games with perfect recall and rising comic control. It is his second novel, and the school stories' high spirits are already his.
an-enemy-of-the-people:
Henrik Ibsen sets his five-act play in a coastal town in southern Norway, in R. Farquharson Sharp's translation. The cast list names Dr. Thomas Stockmann, medical officer of the municipal baths, and his elder brother Peter, mayor of the town and chairman of the baths committee. The doctor has found the town's healing waters poisoned by pollution.

Stockmann expects praise and gets ruin: the mayor, the press, and the town meeting turn on him to protect the baths' income. His daughter Petra stands by him, and Captain Horster offers his house for the famous meeting scene. Alone at the end, Stockmann calls the strongest man the one who stands by himself. The play still serves as the model drama of truth against the crowd.
an-original-belle:
E. P. Roe's An Original Belle opens with a preface on power, which Roe calls the measure of character. The greatest power, he argues, belongs to trained intelligence and moral quality. His heroine Marian begins commonplace enough, a belle of ordinary homage. Circumstances school her to stay honest to her nature and her conscience.

The story culminates in the summer of 1863, Roe's preface says, amid the critical period of the Civil War. Willard Merwyn and Captain Lane stand as the contrasting men of the contents. A scheme of life, a chained will, and a father's forethought shape Marian's probation. Roe sought fairness to the South's motives, he tells its readers directly. The novel uses invasion and battle to test character, not the reverse. Marian's originality is her refusal of the belle's trade: she will be valued for herself, or not at all.
armadale:
Wilkie Collins dedicates his long sensation novel to John Forster. In his preface he warns readers plainly. The story oversteps the limits some critics set for modern fiction, and he is not afraid of his design. Two young men bear the same name, Allan Armadale, bound by a deathbed letter and a shared, guilty inheritance.

The plot runs through a wreck, a Swiss sanatorium, a yachting trip, and London lodgings, driven by Lydia Gwilt, a brilliant and dangerous woman with a forged past. Forged letters, hidden identities, and a plan built on the two Allans' sameness keep the suspense high. Collins sustains the huge machine of coincidence with great skill.
at-the-sign-of-the-eagle:
At the Sign of the Eagle, by Gilbert Parker, opens at a London dinner where two Americans are being weighed. Parker gives the first judgment to Molly, Lady Lawless. Her husband Duke asks what she thinks of their guests. The little man, she says, is affected and servile. The big one strikes her as commanding and rough edged. He looks dangerous in a drawing room, and the more interesting for it.

Business hides behind the invitation. Railways and mines are in play. Lord Hampstead's nephew means to hunt a fortune in the States. Status for dollars is the bargain on the table. Lady Lawless quotes Hamlet at her husband for proposing it. Parker sets American money against English rank in his most social novel. The eagle of the title is the American bird. It has come to roost in Mayfair, and the drawing room must decide what it is worth.
b09-sachs-fastnachtspiele:
Hans Sachs, the Nuremberg shoemaker and master singer, wrote plays for Shrove Tuesday, the carnival before Lent. Four of his Fastnachtspiele, carnival plays, are gathered here in German, from about 1550. The best known of them, Der fahrende Schüler im Paradies, sends a wandering scholar through a comic Paradise.

Carnival plays were short, rowdy, and played by tradesmen for their neighbors in the street. Sachs fills his with sharp talk, mistaken hopes, and fools who get what they earn. The humor is broad, but the craft is real: tight scenes and quick, singing verse. Together the four plays show popular theatre at the height of the Reformation age.
battle-studies-ancient-and-modern-battle:
Colonel Ardant du Picq's Battle Studies examines ancient and modern battle, translated from the eighth French edition by Colonel John N. Greely and Major Robert C. Cotton. Foch's prefatory letter calls Du Picq the champion of moral force, the army's strongest element.

Du Picq argues that moral force preponderates in the outcome of battles, and Foch says American experience in 1918 amply verified his conclusions. The studies draw on ancient warfare and on modern campaigns alike, seeking what actually breaks men in combat. Soldiers and military historians will find Du Picq's analysis of fear, cohesion and leadership still bracing.
bob-son-of-battle:
Alfred Ollivant wrote the great sheepdog novel in this story of Bob, the gray dog of Kenmuir. The book is laid out in six parts, from The Coming of the Tailless Tyke to the final contest for the Shepherds' Trophy. Bob's master is James Moore of Kenmuir, and the dog's rival is Red Wull, the tailless terror owned by the dour Adam McAdam.

Ollivant tells the feud of the two dogs and their masters across years of trials on the Cumberland fells. A sheep-killing mystery hangs over the flock, and suspicion falls where it can do most harm. Chapters of dialect talk among the shepherds carry much of the humour and the grief. The trophy competition decides the rivalry in public, but the black killer plot must be settled first, in darkness.
born-in-exile:
George Gissing's Born in Exile follows Godwin Peak, a clever boy born to a struggling shopkeeper's family. The story opens at Whitelaw College on a summer day in 1874. Peak's father kept a small cottage household on two pounds a week. The boy's militant egoism, his hunger to rise, grows with his schooling.

Peak wins scholarships yet feels exiled among gentlemen by his birth. He falls in love with Sidwell Warricombe, a clergyman's daughter of sincere faith. To win her world he feigns religious belief he does not hold. His friend Earwaker watches the deception with unease. Gissing writes a pitiless study of class shame and intellectual pride. Peak's exile is self-made, and the novel asks whether a man can lie his way into belonging.
bulfinch-s-mythology-the-age-of-fable:
Thomas Bulfinch wrote The Age of Fable to retell the myths of Greece and Rome for general readers, and the Reverend E E Hale revised this edition. Bulfinch aimed at readers who met mythological names in poetry and art without knowing the stories. Greek and Roman gods stand at the center. Their Latin and Greek names are explained as the tales proceed.

Early chapters cover creation, the golden age, Prometheus, and Pandora. Stories follow Apollo and Daphne, Pyramus and Thisbe, and Phaeton driving the sun's chariot. Midas, Baucis and Philemon, Cupid and Psyche, and the founding of Thebes come later. Bulfinch retells each tale in clear, calm prose and links many to later poems. Readers get the classic nineteenth-century doorway into classical myth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-font:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Fontenelle, or the Abbey of Saint Wandrille, describes a Benedictine monastery in Normandy near Caudebec. St. Wandrille came of Austrasia's royal family and stood high at Dagobert the First's court. He retired to Montfaucon in 629, spent time at Bobbio and Romainmôtier, and returned to Normandy to found his monastery in 648.

He built a great St. Peter's basilica almost three hundred feet in length, consecrated by St. Ouen in 657. Fire destroyed it in 756, Abbot Ansegisus rebuilt it with narthex and tower, and Danish pirates wrecked it about 862, scattering the monks for over a century through Chartres, Boulogne and St. Omer. The entry follows the community's long exile and eventual return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-patri:
Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, first appears as orphanotrophos, the dignitary entrusted with the care of orphans in the church of Constantinople. That post carried high rank and curial influence, and he made the most of it. Suidas describes a striking personality: engaging magnificence of manner, openhanded, suave yet noble in bearing, courtly in speech, and fond of ecclesiastical display. When Patriarch Gennadius died in 471, he succeeded him.

For five or six years his episcopate was uneventful. Change came when the usurping Emperor Basiliscus, won over to Eutychian teaching by Timotheus Aelurus, issued an encyclical rejecting the Council of Chalcedon. Acacius at first hesitated over adding his name to the new course. He died in 489, and his schism outlived him some thirty years, ending only with Emperor Justin's return to unity under Pope Hormisdas in 519.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aci-reale:
Aci-Reale, or Jaca Regalis, is a Sicilian diocese over fourteen communes in Catania's civil province, immediately subject to Rome. Gregory XVI created it in 1844; Monsignor Gerlando Maria Genuardi of the Oratory became its first bishop only in 1872. The episcopal city stands picturesquely at Mount Etna's foot, amid rich orange and almond gardens.

The diocese counts 18 parishes and 305 churches, served by 330 secular priests and 70 regulars, among 150,219 inhabitants. The entry cites Cappelletti, Gams, Vigo, and Pirri, and notes the controversy over the cult of St. Expedite, treated in Civilta Cattolica and the Analecta Bollandiana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrianople:
Adrianople is a city of Turkey in Europe, said by legend to have been built by Orestes, son of Agamemnon, at the meeting of the Tonsus and Ardiscus with the Hebrus. Emperor Hadrian developed and adorned it with monuments, renaming Orestias as Hadrianopolis, and made it capital of Haemimont, or Thrace. Constantine defeated Licinius there in 323, and Valens was killed by the Goths there in 378.

Theodore of Epirus seized it in 1227 during the Latin Empire, and Asen of Bulgaria killed him there two years later. Murad I captured it in 1360, and it served as Turkish capital from 1362 to 1453. Russians occupied it in 1829 and again in 1878, in wars for Greek and Bulgarian independence. Today it heads a vilayet of about 960,000 people, trading in woven stuffs, silks, carpets, and farm products, and it holds the grand mosque of Selim II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-affinity-in-t:
Scripture treats affinity as a bar to wedlock, evident from Leviticus 18 and 20. Unlike church affinity, which arises from lawful and unlawful intercourse alike, biblical affinity springs from betrothal only, which among Hebrews scarcely differed from ratified marriage. The Leviticus texts bar direct-line marriage with a stepmother, stepdaughter, grand-stepdaughter, mother-in-law, and daughter-in-law.

In the collateral line they bar marriage with a paternal uncle's wife, with a sister-in-law except where the levirate law applies, and with a wife's sister while the former wife lives. Jews held the wife's relation to her husband's family closer than the husband's to his wife's. Leviticus 20 sanctions these rules: death threatens direct-line transgressors, while childlessness threatens collateral ones, meaning offspring counted illegitimate or assigned to the dead uncle or brother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aisle:
Aisle, from Latin ala and Old French aile, is in architecture one of a church's lateral divisions, separated from the nave by piers, pillars, or columns in rows. Sometimes a church has only one side aisle. Often the aisle continues around the apse. Occasionally aisles stop at the transepts. Very large churches' transepts may have three aisles.

Gothic architecture's rule puts aisle roofs well below the nave roof, admitting light through clerestory windows. In most Romanesque churches aisle roofs are but little lower than the nave's. The aisle generally has one story, though occasionally an upper one, sometimes used as a gallery. Chichester, Milan, and Amiens have five, Antwerp and Paris seven, and Cordova cathedral in Spain nineteen. Aisles existed in Roman basilicas and in most Christian churches of all periods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-de-l-is:
Alain de l'Isle, also Alain of Lille, Alanus ab Insulis, or de Insulis, was a monk, poet, preacher, theologian, and eclectic philosopher, born about 1128, probably at Lille, whence his name. He died at Citeaux in 1203. He is believed to have studied and taught in Paris for some time before joining the Third Council of the Lateran in 1179.

In his day Alain won extraordinary celebrity as teacher and learned man, called Alain the Great and the Universal Doctor. Legend tells of a scholar crying that his dialectical opponent was either Alain or the devil. His principal work, Ars Fidei Catholicae, dedicated to Clement III, refutes with rational argument the errors of Mohammedans, Jews, and heretics. He also wrote Tractatus Contra Haereticos and Theologicae Regulae. He also wrote two poems, De Planctu Naturae and Anticlaudianus. His theology blends rationalism with mysticism, and he ranks among medieval writers who influenced Dante.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-cas:
Albert of Castile was a Dominican historian born about 1460 and dead in 1522. He joined the Dominican order young at the Venice house of Sts. John and Paul and became skilled in nearly every branch of learning of his day, with history as his chief study. His own works include catalogues of the illustrious men and the saints of his order, both printed at Venice in 1501.

His short chronicle of the order, printed in 1504, traces the popes, the Dominican generals, and the order's notable men from its foundation, drawing chiefly on Giacomo de Luzato. Castile also edited a Latin Bible with full apparatus printed at Venice in 1506. He re-edited it fifteen years later with a concordance, an index to the words of both Testaments. He also edited the order's constitutions and other liturgical books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-de-toc:
Alexis de Tocqueville was a French writer and statesman, born at Verneuil in July 1805 and dead at Cannes in April 1859. His great-grandfather was Malesherbes, who defended Louis XVI. While judging at Versailles in 1830 he befriended Gustave de Beaumont, and the two travelled to America, where Tocqueville studied the penitentiary system and democracy.

Two books came from the journey: a joint work on the American penitentiary system. Tocqueville's own Democracy in America appeared in two volumes, in 1835 and 1840. The book won him seats in the Academy of Moral and Political Sciences in 1838 and the French Academy in 1841. As deputy for Valognes he sat with the opposition. He served the Second Republic as vice-president of the Legislative Assembly and foreign minister in 1849. Under the Empire he wrote The Old Regime and the Revolution, whose first part appeared in 1856.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-stole: The altar stole was a medieval ornament shaped like the ends of a stole and fixed to the altar's front. It borrowed the stole's form for display rather than wear, marking the altar itself with a priestly emblem. Medieval altars thus carried a familiar vestment shape as pure ornament alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-lisle:
Ambrose Lisle March Phillipps de Lisle was born 17 March 1809 and died 5 March 1878, son of Charles March Phillipps of Garendon Park and Harriet Ducarel of Huguenot descent. He took the de Lisle name in 1862 on inheriting the family's estates at his father's death. Brought up Anglican, he met the émigré Abbé Giraud at school, whose holy life clashed with what he had heard of Catholics. A Paris visit in 1823 introduced him to Catholic liturgy.

He persuaded his Anglican rector to set a cross on the communion table, promptly suppressed by Peterborough's bishop as savouring of Popery. He later devoted persistent energy and faith to Catholicism's spread, through material help and spiritual means he valued more strongly. The rest of his life passed without special incident, though he stayed active in public affairs touching the Church's fortunes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amende-honora:
The amende honorable was an obsolete French church form of honorary satisfaction, lasting into the seventeenth century. The name itself marks the act: honourable amends offered openly, not privately. Performed at the ecclesiastical judge's bidding within his court's precinct, it could once be enforced at the church door or another public place. It fell ordinarily only on condemned criminals, who came stripped to the shirt, barefoot and bareheaded, candle in hand, begging pardon of God, the king, and justice.

Its public, barefoot, candle-lit form made the penance itself the satisfaction, performed where justice sat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amiel-weeks-w:
Amiel Weeks Whipple, military engineer and soldier, was born at Greenwich, Massachusetts, in 1818 and died at Washington in 1863. Son of David and Abigail Pepper Whipple, he studied at Amherst, graduated West Point in 1841, and surveyed the Patapsco, New Orleans approaches, and Portsmouth Harbour. He later fixed parts of the Canadian and Mexican boundaries, and in 1853 led Pacific railroad explorations near the 35th parallel.

Becoming Catholic around 1857 in Detroit lighthouse service, he engineered under McDowell and McClellan, his maps serving many Virginian battlefields. As brigadier-general of volunteers in 1862 he defended Washington's Virginia side and fought gallantly at Antietam and Fredericksburg. He was mortally wounded by a sharpshooter at Chancellorsville, receiving the last rites on the field. Breveted brigadier-general on 4 May, major-general of volunteers on 6 May, and major-general by brevet on 7 May, he died hours later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancren-riwle:
Ancren Riwle is a thirteenth-century rule for anchoresses. In Middle English ancren meant solitaries of either sex. This rule speaks only to ladies who left the world for a secluded religious life. Several copies survive. One, at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, bears the title Ancren Wisse. Some take it for an abridgment of Simon of Ghent's Latin tract. Simon was Bishop of Salisbury from 1297 to 1315.

The British Museum holds five copies. Three served Morton's Camden Society edition of 1852. Morton rejects the idea that the English text translates Simon of Ghent. He judges Cotton Cleopatra C vi the English original. The rule orders a day given mostly to prayer, with Litany and Office for the Dead. Its author admits the life, with the ten old Commandments, is hard. Yet he adds that nothing is so hard that love does not make it tender, soft, and sweet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animals-in-th:
The Bible makes no pretensions to science, so it holds no elaborate classification. The sacred books were composed by and for a pastoral people in constant communication with nature. To such a people, references to animals are natural, and the more animals abounded, the more frequent they are. In fact, over a hundred and twenty species are named in the Scriptures.

How animal references are introduced, their frequency, and their documents' dates may show the country's conditions at different stages of its history. The article proceeds species by species, weighing Hebrew names against Palestine's fauna. Entries run from the camel, reckoned unclean among the Jews, to the camelopardalus of Deuteronomy, combining camel and leopard for the giraffe. This translation is doubtless erroneous, since neither giraffe nor chamois lived in Palestine. Further entries cover the cankerworm, the locust in its larva state, and the cat, mentioned only once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-teril:
Anthony Terill, born Bonville, was an English theologian from Canford, born in 1623 and died at Liège in 1676. His Catholic mother and faith-estranged father raised him in heresy until fifteen, when he converted and left England as Terill. He studied about three years at Saint Omer's English College, then began priesthood studies at Rome's English College.

Two months after ordination he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Saint Andrea. After his noviceship he served as penitentiary at Loreto, professor at Florence and Parma, then theology and mathematics professor at Liège, and rector there for three years. He wrote Conclusiones philosophicæ (1657), Problema mathematico-philosophicum (1660), Fundamentum totius theologiæ moralis (1668), and Regula morum (1677, posthumous). The last two made him a moral theologian: the Fundamentum defends probabilism, and the Regula morum answers objections from Concina, Elizalde, and other Rigorists. Amort calls him eruditissimum et probabilistarum antsignanum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-perre:
Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, a statesman cardinal born in 1517, served two Habsburg emperors across a long career. Son of Charles the Fifth's chief minister, he studied at Padua and Louvain and became bishop of Arras at twenty-one. He spoke for the emperor at the Council of Trent and helped settle the Peace of Crepy and the marriage of Philip the Second to Mary Tudor.

Under Philip Philip raised him to Mechlin's archbishopric in 1559, and to the cardinalate two years later, guiding the Netherlands as chief counsellor to Margaret of Parma. Unpopular with local nobles, he left Brussels, yet his vast correspondence, edited in many volumes, still records Habsburg policy in detail. The entry portrays a tireless minister whose pen shaped an empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apsidiole: An apsidiole, also written absidiale, is a small or secondary apse. It is one of the apses flanking the main apse in a three-apse church. It may also be an apse chapel projecting outside the church, above all when the projection itself resembles an apse in shape. Bond, writing on Gothic architecture in England, notes that the Norman plan of the eastern limb brought to England at the Conquest held a central apse flanked by apsidioles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristotle:
Aristotle, called here the greatest of pagan philosophers, was born at Stagira, a Greek colony in Chalcidice, in 384 BC and died at Chalcis in Euboea in 322 BC. His father Nicomachus served as court physician to King Amyntas of Macedonia, a post his ancestors had held, so medicine ran in the family. That background likely shaped the young Aristotle's turn toward investigating natural phenomena when, at eighteen, he went to Athens.

From eighteen to thirty-seven he stayed at Athens as Plato's pupil, distinguished among those who gathered in the Grove of Academus near Plato's house. Legends about teacher and pupil abound, many painting Aristotle in a harsh light. The article sets those tales beside the record of a mind that ranged over logic, nature, ethics, and politics. Readers get the life that underlies the system later Christians both used and debated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armidale:
Armidale is a diocese in New South Wales, Australia, with Armidale's cathedral, 335 miles north of Sydney, and one of six suffragan sees in the Sydney province. Its borders run from Queensland in the north to Lismore diocese in the east, Wilcannia ten miles beyond Walgett in the west, and Maitland and Bathurst in the south. They cover about 85,000 square miles. Armidale became a municipality only in 1863.

Ten years earlier, in 1853, Timothy McCarthy became its first resident priest, in a thinly settled farming and grazing district where Catholics lived few and far apart. McCarthy made Armidale his headquarters, and his missionary district, Cardinal Moran says, stretched to the Queensland border and the Pacific Ocean. His tours lasted three months, from the Tweed down to the Richmond, then to the Clarence, on to Walcha, and across the Liverpool ranges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astronomy-in-:
Astronomy in the Bible begins from a negative: Jews made no systematic observations of heavenly bodies. Astral worship was rife in Palestine, and close attention to its objects risked yielding to its seductions. Astronomy therefore stayed inseparable from star worship, and prophets' anathemas against it were not careless. As the Almighty's most glorious works, celestial lights are celebrated in scripture in passages thrilling with rapture, but practical appeal to them shrank to a minimum.

Even regulating times and seasons stayed largely empirical. Jews used a lunar year, beginning for religious purposes with the new moon following the spring equinox, normally twelve months or 354 days. Since festivals were partly agricultural, the calendar also depended on the sun's course, and some adjustment was needed to fit lunar months to solar seasons. The entry follows that calendar problem through biblical texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auriesville:
Auriesville is the site of the Mohawk village in Montgomery County, New York, where Father Isaac Jogues and his companions Goupil and Lalande were killed for the faith. It stands on the south bank of the Mohawk, about forty miles west of Albany. The name comes from Auries, the last Mohawk there, while the Indians called the village Ossernenon, also Gandawaga. Jogues and Goupil were brought there as prisoners in 1642, and Jogues returned with Lalande in 1646.

Bressani was tortured there in 1644, and after Le Moyne's peace embassy a permanent mission rose in 1667. Fathers such as Lamberville, Fremin, and Bruyas labored there until the mission was destroyed in 1684. The Indian girl Tegakwitha was born at the village and later escaped to Canada. Pilgrims still gather in summer, often four or five thousand strong, fasting and receiving Communion at the shrine. The buildings are temporary, pending the Church's judgment on the martyrdoms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-authenticity-:
The authenticity of the Bible, this short entry argues, is twofold, because its authorship is twofold. First, the books of the Bible are authentic in the human sense: they enjoy all the natural authority due to their respective human authors. That first kind of authenticity must be weighed book by book, and the entry sends readers to the articles on the several books of Scripture for those cases.

Second, the books hold a higher authenticity, because a divine, supernatural authority clothes them through divine authorship. They are, in the entry's terms, the inspired word of God. That second sense springs from biblical inspiration itself, and the entry points to the article on Inspiration for its full defense. The piece is thus a brief map of a larger argument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barocco-style:
Barocco, French baroque, is a debased application of Renaissance features to architecture. The term also marks bad taste in design and ornament generally. Carlo Maderna, Bernini, and Borromini rank among its most famous practitioners. Leading examples are Maderna's Santa Maria della Vittoria and Borromini's Santa Agnese, both at Rome.

Naples is full of baroque churches, though a few, like the Gesù Nuovo, are dignified and creditable designs. Longhena's domical Santa Maria della Salute at Venice stands majestic and in excellent style. Three Venetian churches, San Barnaba, San Basso, and San Moise, show three different baroque types. The style ruled church architecture for nearly two centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belleville:
Belleville is a diocesan entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, covering the southern Illinois diocese created in 1887. Its territory runs across the southern counties of the state, carved out of the older Diocese of Alton after its bishop died. John Janssen, once vicar-general at Alton, became its first bishop in 1888.

Statistics anchor the entry, listing parishes, clergy, schools, and church buildings at the diocese's founding and in its later years. Growth in priests, parishes, and Catholic schools shows a young diocese filling out its map. The piece reads as a snapshot of church organization on the American prairie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury, was the last Plantagenet of her line to fall to Henry VIII. She was executed in 1541 after her son Reginald denounced the king's divorce. Born in 1473, she was the daughter of George, Duke of Clarence. She married Richard Pole, was widowed in 1505, and was restored by Henry VIII as countess and governess to Princess Mary.

Her favor ended when Reginald, then in exile, sent Henry his treatise defending church unity and attacking the divorce. Though Margaret and her eldest son rebuked Reginald, Henry struck at the family in England. Two sons were arrested for treason in 1538, and Margaret herself was put to death on Tower Green on 27 May 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brownsville:
Brownsville, a vicariate apostolic erected in 1874, covers 22,391 square miles of lower Texas along the Rio Grande. Before that date all Texas lay under Galveston. The state then split into Galveston north of the Colorado, San Antonio between the Colorado and Nueces, and Brownsville southward. Brownsville took Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr, Zapata, and Webb counties with others north of the Nueces.

Its chief towns are Laredo with 12,000 people, Brownsville with 8,000, and Corpus Christi with 7,000, amid a total of about 110,000, including 79,000 Catholics, mostly Mexican, and 3,000 English-speaking Catholics. Indians held the land less than sixty years before. Brownsville began with Major Brown in the Mexican War, and its church rose in 1852. Oblate fathers, settled in 1852, mission from San Ignacio to the river's mouth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burchard-of-b:
Burchard of Basle, an eleventh-century bishop and loyal partisan of Henry IV, fought the pope's cause with sword and council. Born to the counts of Neuenburg about mid-century, he became Bishop of Basle in 1072 through Henry's favor and served as a foremost royal adviser. He aided Henry against the Saxons in 1073 and 1075, then joined the Worms assembly of January 1076 that proclaimed Gregory VII deposed and wrote him an insulting letter.

With Huzmann of Speyer he won Lombard bishops at Piacenza to renounce Gregory, earning excommunication and deposition at the Lenten synod of 1076. He walked with Henry to Canossa in January 1077 and regained his office. In the civil war against Rudolf of Swabia he fought repeatedly, suffered crushing defeat in 1078 and barely escaped, then ravaged Swabia with cruel soldiery until Rudolf fell dead in 1080. Henry rewarded him with land, and he died on 12 April 1107.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canticle:
Canticle is the English Catholic Bible's word for the Vulgate's canticum when it means a sacred song. Other uses of the same Latin word appear simply as song. The distinction matters because the Authorized Version translates from Hebrew and Greek and calls everything song. It does not mark the sacred cases apart.

Seven Old Testament canticles from the Breviary serve at Lauds through the week. Sundays use the Canticle of the Three Children, and Saturdays use the Canticle of Moses. New Testament canticles join them, including Zachary's at Lauds. The entry also notes English usage, where the Prayer Book restricts the word to the Benedicite. Its calendar applies Canticles to the Song of Solomon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-captain-in-th:
Captain in the Douay Bible stands for several different Hebrew and Latin words covering both civil and military officers. The entry warns that the rendering follows no fixed rule. The same Hebrew or Latin term may appear as captain in one place and under another word elsewhere. That holds for the Vulgate as well as for the Hebrew and Greek texts.

Civil uses are rare and reserved for the highest offices, such as captain of my people. Military uses run through every grade, from captains of the host and of thousands to captains of hundreds, fifties, and tens. Chariot captains, cavalry commanders, and bodyguard chiefs complete the range. In the New Testament the word occurs only once, in Matthew's quotation of Micah's promise of a captain to rule Israel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlisle:
Carlisle was an ancient English diocese, smaller than the present Anglican diocese enlarged in 1856. Its territory first became a political unit under William Rufus. He made it the Earldom of Carlisle from most of Cumberland and Westmoreland. Under Henry I the earldom became a bishopric, after belonging to Durham with a strong Celtic element looking to Glasgow.

Henry secured his former confessor Æthelwulf, an Augustinian prior, as first bishop in 1133, and Æthelwulf ruled until 1156, building a Norman minster whose transepts and nave survive in part. His Augustinian canons served the cathedral, an arrangement unusual in England. The entry closes with a plundered diocese, a single archdeaconry, and a cathedral first dedicated to the Virgin and later, at the Reformation, to the Holy Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-epis:
The Catholic Epistles are the letter of St. James, the letter of St. Jude, two letters of St. Peter, and the first three letters of St. John. They carry the name Catholic because, unlike the letters of St. Paul, they were written not to one person or church but to the faithful in general, in the manner of an encyclical letter.

The name reaches a little further than the address alone would suggest. The other two letters of St. John, though written to particular persons, also carry the name Catholic, since they have always been shelved with the letters bearing it. The entry is short, but it fixes the meaning of a term readers meet throughout the New Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-saint:
An entry on Charles Sainte-Claire Deville, a French geologist who studied volcanoes and built France's weather service. Born at St. Thomas in the West Indies in 1814, he trained at the Paris School of Mines and began with explorations in the Antilles, studying earthquakes and eruptions. Visits to Vesuvius and Stromboli in the late 1850s fed his theory that eruptions come from sea water entering cracks in the earth's crust and meeting hot rock.

Deville joined the Academy of Sciences in 1857, assisted Elie de Beaumont at the Collège de France, succeeding him as professor in 1875. As inspector general of the Meteorological Service from 1872, he set up a chain of weather stations across France and Algeria and became first president of the Montsouris observatory. He also worked in chemistry, analysing minerals and studying molecular physics, before his death in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chasuble:
An entry on the chasuble, the chief and most visible vestment worn by a priest at Mass, covering all the rest. In Latin it is called casula or planeta. Liturgical dress grew from ordinary Roman clothing, with garments set aside, newer and cleaner, for sacred use. The chasuble itself began as the common outer cloak of the lower orders, a square or round cloth with a hole for the head.

Its name means little house, since like a small cottage it covers the whole person. Over time the garment narrowed, and the French type grew less ample and often stiff, with a cross on the back. Medieval crosses often took a Y shape for reasons of cut rather than symbol. Before use the chasuble is blessed, and at ordination the bishop calls it the priestly vestment signifying charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chile:
A wide-ranging entry on Chile, the narrow strip of South American coast between the Pacific and the Andes. It runs some 2,500 miles from latitude 17 degrees south to Cape Horn, varying from 185 to 100 miles in width. Peaks rise over 22,000 feet, more than forty volcanoes dot the range, and the north is arid while the south is cold and timbered, with glaciers reaching the sea. Its minerals include gold, silver, copper, iron, nitrates, and coal.

Church life forms one part of the survey. Chile makes a single ecclesiastical province, with the Archdiocese of Santiago and the sees of Concepción, Ancud, and Serena, plus the vicariates of Tarapacá and Antofagasta. Indian missions in the south are run by Franciscans, Capuchins, and Salesians, religious orders staff many schools and colleges, and religious teaching is compulsory even in public schools. The entry also traces the country's peoples and history from before 1535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronicon-pas:
An entry on the Chronicon Paschale, the Paschal Chronicle, a valuable Byzantine world chronicle of the seventh century. It takes its name from its system of Christian chronology, built on the paschal canon, the cycle for fixing Easter. It is also called the Alexandrine, Antiochene, Casaubonian, Constantinopolitan chronicle, or the Sicilian Fasti.

Its anonymous author titled it an epitome spanning Adam, the first man, to the twentieth year of the emperor Heraclius and the nineteenth consulship of his son Constantine. Like other Byzantine chronicles it follows Eusebius, beginning with Creation and running to its own day. Written in the plain but ornate idiom of common life, it mixes church history with anecdotes, portraits, earthquakes, and comets for monks and ordinary readers of the Eastern Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commentaries-:
Cornelius Aherne's vast survey admits at the start that a full history of exegesis would fill many volumes. Even Dante, a recent writer, had drawn thirteen hundred commentaries by 1900. So Aherne gives only the barest outline, with a bibliography to lead readers further. He touches the high points of Jewish, patristic, medieval, and modern commentaries, both Catholic and non-Catholic. Jewish writing comes first, since it leads naturally into Christian exegesis.

That Jewish section runs through Philo, the Targums, the Mishna and Talmuds, and the Midrashim. Hillel and Shammai, the last of the paired teachers, anchor the Mishna tradition, while later rabbis debated its text for generations. Patristic, medieval, and modern writers follow in turn, each age reading Scripture through its own tools. The entry serves as a map: a reader can grasp the whole field's shape, then follow its bibliography into any period or school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordances-:
John Francis Fenlon's entry defines Bible concordances as verbal indexes: lists of Bible words in alphabetical order, pointing to every passage where each word occurs. A good concordance quotes enough of each passage to jog the memory of one who knows it. Subject indexes exist too, but English usage means a verbal concordance, a text-finder. It helps every Bible student locate a half-remembered text from a single important word. Fenlon calls it useful, indeed indispensable.
