Verbal concordances began with Dominican friars for Latin. Hebrew's first came from Mordecai or Isaac Nathan, worked on from 1438 to 1448. Greek Septuagint concordances start with Kircher in 1607 and Tromm in 1718. Greek New Testament pioneers include Betulius in 1546, Estienne in 1594, and Schmid in 1638. Syriac rests on Schaaf's Lexicon of 1709. English concordances arose in the mid-sixteenth century. No concordance to the English Catholic Bible then existed, save for deutero-canonical books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantinopl:
Siméon Vailhé's entry follows Constantinople, city of Constantine, Byzantine, now Ottoman, capital. The modern city holds one of the world's finest sites, joining Europe with Asia. It links the Black Sea and Southern Russia with greater Europe and Asia. Water surrounds it except on the west, guarded by walls. Its sea front runs about eight miles, air generally pure, climate very temperate.

A special district in three sections, two European and one Asian, frames the city. Stamboul borders the Sea of Marmora, while Galata and Pera form European quarters. The Bosporus, about eighteen miles long, separates Europe from Asia. Early history traces Byzantium's founding; the Christian city took the name Constantinople by 324. Constantine chose it as the Empire's new capital, though wars kept him away. Church prosperity matched political grandeur, with rich churches and court luxury exciting covetousness. Heresy and schism follow, Photius leading the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ba:
The Council of Basle, convoked by Martin V in 1431 and closed at Lausanne in 1449, grew from the wounds of the Avignon papacy and the Great Western Schism. Rival claimants for St Peter's throne had shaken faith in monarchical church government. Reformers looked to a council for remedy. Reform of the Church in head and members, peace among nations, and settlement of the Hussite wars stood as its purposes.

Quarrels with Eugene IV over presidency and dissolution split the assembly, which declared a council superior to a pope, deposed Eugene, and elected the antipope Felix V. The rump at Basle faded into schism while the council's ideas lived on, feeding Gallicanism in France through the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges and preparing German minds for severance from Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-cons:
A biographical entry presents Cuthbert Constable, formerly Tunstall, who died on 27 March 1746. Son of Francis Tunstall of Wycliffe Hall, he inherited the Burton Constable estates in 1718 on his uncle's death and changed his surname to Constable. Educated at Douai, he studied medicine at Montpellier and took a doctorate.

At Burton Constable he built a large collection of books and manuscripts and became a steady patron of Catholic letters. He lent documents to Bishop Challoner for his Memoirs of Missionary Priests and helped fund Dodd's History of the Church of England. His papers hold correspondence with Oxford scholars, above all on Abraham Woodhead, whom he revered. His only publication was a life of Woodhead prefixed to an edition of Woodhead's work in 1736.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-noble:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Noble, a Manchester physician born in 1810 and dead in 1885. Son of a Preston Catholic family, he was apprenticed to a surgeon. He joined the Royal College of Surgeons, and began practice in Manchester in 1834. There he soon developed the keen interest in mental disease that marked his career.

His first work, an essay on estimating human character, made him president of the Manchester Phrenological Society. Later books covered manufactures and health, the brain and its physiology, and psychological medicine, including a study of insanity. He married in 1840, fathered eight children, one the novelist Frances Noble, and became a fellow of the College of Physicians in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desert-in-the:
An entry on the Hebrew words that the Douay Bible renders as desert or wilderness, and why they differ from the English idea. No Sahara-like waste is meant: these tracts gave pasture for flocks and sheltered nomads, not settled towns. Four words carry the sense, each with its own shade, and the entry works through them one by one.

Midbar, the most general term, comes from a root meaning to lead cattle to pasture. Arabah names an arid steppe plain, Horbah a place lying waste, and Jeshimon a waterless waste. Chief biblical deserts follow, from the Exodus tract to Sin, Sinai, Cades, and Pharan, and the temptation of Christ is placed, tentatively, in the Arabah west of the Jordan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-disciple:
Disciple most often means one who learns an art or science from a master. The word comes from the Latin discipulus, though the English sense is narrower, setting disciple against master as scholar stands to teacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Old Testament uses the word only once, in Isaiah. Yet the idea appears when writers speak of sons of the prophets and of children in the wisdom books.

The New Testament uses disciple far more freely, first for pupils of a teacher and then for converts and believers, men and women alike. Even the half-taught folk Saint Paul found at Ephesus bear the name. The entry thus maps a word that grew from the classroom into the very title of the Christian believer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domicile:
Domicile, in canon law, is the right of dwelling or residence, borrowed from Roman law and refined by the Church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that canon law holds no home-grown theory of domicile. Both canon law and modern civil codes took the Roman doctrine, while canon law added the notion of quasi-domicile, a second home with legal weight.

For centuries church law made no special rule on domicile, bending to Roman and barbarian custom. Only in the thirteenth century, after Bologna revived Roman law study, did legists and canonists bring the Roman theory into the schools and then into practice. The entry traces that reception and its bearing on marriage, benefices, and church courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donatus-of-fi:
Donatus of Fiesole was an Irish teacher, poet, and bishop who ruled from about 829 to 876. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry draws on an old collection of lives of the fathers, copied in the eleventh century at Florence. Irish-born of a noble house, Donatus visited the apostles' tombs at Rome about 816. Journeying north, providence led him to Fiesole as the people prayed for a bishop.

Raised by popular acclaim to the see, he revived piety and learning in his church and taught the art of metrical composition himself. He also wrote verse praising his homeland and its people, and an epitaph recalling his Irish birth, his service to the princes of Italy, and his teaching of grammar and poetry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-douay-bible:
The Douay Bible is the English Catholic version on which nearly all later English Catholic Bibles still rest. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces it to the religious wars of the sixteenth century, when Protestant versions, used as weapons of debate, showed signs of controversial bias in their renderings. English Catholics needed a translation of their own, exact and fit to appeal to in argument.

The English College at Douai in Flanders took up the task; William Allen had founded it in 1568. Doctor Gregory Martin carried the chief share. Challoner's revision of 1749 became the standard text in most later editions, while Archbishop Kenrick's independent revision served America from 1849 to 1859. The entry thus tells the birth of the English Catholic Bible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-droit-de-rega:
Droit de regale, the right of regality, first meant all rights belonging to the king alone. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry splits them into greater rights, essential to sovereignty such as royal authority, and lesser rights, such as hunting, fishing, and mining. By abuse, rulers of the Middle Ages and later claimed the income of vacant sees and imperial abbeys, and the phrase narrowed to that seized right.

On what ground rulers claimed the income is disputed, whether from sovereignty itself, from investiture, or from feudal tenure. The entry weighs these views and points to the long quarrel with the papacy, above all under Innocent the Eleventh and Louis the Fourteenth. It cites Stutz, Michelet, and Mention among the scholars of the dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-editions-of-t:
Editions of the Bible, in this entry, means the printed reproductions of its original texts. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets aside both manuscript copies of the originals and printed or written versions, which have their own articles. Since the original text was written in Hebrew or Greek, with small Aramaic portions counted with the Hebrew, the study follows the printed Hebrew and Greek texts from their first presses onward.

The entry explains the critical marks and symbols by which Bible codices are denoted, a system set out more fully under Biblical Criticism. It closes with the great modern editors, from Gregory's Text Criticism to Von Soden's writings on the oldest reachable form of the New Testament. For students of the Bible's text, it is a map of print after centuries of hand copying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eduard-von-st:
Eduard von Steinle was an Austrian historical painter of the Romantic school, born at Vienna in 1810 and dead at Frankfurt in 1886. He learned from Kupelwieser, Overbeck, and Cornelius, and took in the new German manner formed at Rome, though he chose to work in Germany. Early commissions took him to Rheineck Castle chapel and to Frankfurt's Hall of Emperors, where he painted Albert I and Ferdinand III.

From 1850 he taught historical painting at Frankfurt's Stadel Institute. He left more than a hundred religious panel pictures and cartoons for church windows, and he painted great fresco cycles at Klein-Heubach, Munster, Aachen, and Cologne Cathedral. Critics praised his detail but felt his wall work lacked the broad, monumental sweep such painting needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphanius-of:
Epiphanius of Constantinople was Patriarch of that city from 520 until his death in 535. He followed John II at a turning point: the reaction against Monophysitism that came with the accession of the Catholic emperor Justin I in 518. Justin let the Henotikon of Zeno quietly drop, and a synod of forty bishops under John II proclaimed Chalcedon across the empire and deposed Monophysite bishops.

That synod also reopened talks with Rome after the Acacian schism of 484 to 519. On Easter Day, 24 March 519, reunion was proclaimed, and Monophysite leaders fled to Egypt. When John died in 520, Epiphanius succeeded him with papal authority to reconcile schismatics who retracted and signed Pope Hormisdas's formula. He signed it himself first, and four of his letters to Hormisdas survive, with the pope's replies, showing his eagerness for communion with Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euphemius-of-:
Euphemius was Patriarch of Constantinople from 490 to 496, during the Acacian schism that split East and West for thirty-five years. The breach began when Emperor Zeno's Henotikon of 482 tried to please both sides. It held to Nicaea and Constantinople while passing over Chalcedon and its teaching on Christ's two natures. Euphemius, who followed Acacius and his successor, set out to heal the wound.

He recognized Chalcedon, put the pope's name back in the diptychs, the lists read aloud in the liturgy, and broke with Peter Mongus of Alexandria. Yet he would not strike the names of Acacius and his own predecessor from those lists, and Rome refused communion on any other terms. Later he made Emperor Anastasius sign a Catholic profession of faith. The emperor turned on him, had him accused of treason, deposed him in 496, and sent him into exile, where he died at Ancyra in 515.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fiesole:
Fiesole is a Tuscan diocese, suffragan of the archdiocese of Florence. Of ancient Etruscan origin, it once outdid Florence in power in the valley below. Sulla colonised it, and the Florentines sacked it in 1010 and 1025. Its cathedral of St Romulus, built in 1028, holds notable sculptures by Mino da Fiesole.

St Donatus, an Irish monk and bishop from 826, advised the emperors Louis the Pious and Lothair. St Andrew Corsini, bishop from 1352, won fame as a peacemaker between individuals and states. Fra Angelico, called da Fiesole, trained in its Dominican house of San Domenico. The diocese counted 254 parishes and some 155,800 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-council:
The First Council of Constantinople met in May 381, called by Emperor Theodosius. Its aims were a Catholic line at Constantinople, the Nicene faith, and an end to Macedonian heresy. Some 150 Catholic and 36 dissenting bishops attended, first under Meletius of Antioch. After Meletius died, Gregory Nazianzen and then Nectarius presided in turn.

The council confirmed Gregory as bishop and issued the famous Constantinopolitan creed. That creed, likely a Jerusalem form of words from 369 to 373, stressed the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Its first canon condemned Arianism, Macedonianism, and Apollinarianism in all their shades. Its third canon gave Constantinople honour second only to Old Rome, a rank Rome long resisted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fourth-counci:
The Fourth Council of Constantinople, counted as the Eighth General Council, opened on 5 October 869 in the cathedral of Hagia Sophia under legates of Pope Adrian II. It grew out of a decade of turmoil in which Photius had displaced Patriarch Ignatius and tried to depose Pope Nicholas I. When the emperor Basil the Macedonian took power in 867, Photius was confined to a monastery, Ignatius was recalled, and both emperor and patriarch asked Rome for a general council.

Never more than 102 bishops attended. The council made them sign the formula of Pope Hormisdas, pledging to follow the Apostolic See of Rome. It reconciled bishops who had sided with Photius, heard Photius himself in silence or brief answers, renewed his excommunication, and banished him to a monastery on the Bosporus. Its twenty-seven canons also condemned the last traces of iconoclasm and interference by civil rulers in church affairs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vata:
Francois Vatable, better called Watebled and also written Gastebled or Ouateble, was a French Hellenist and Hebraist born at Gamaches in Picardy, probably late in the fifteenth century. He died at Paris on 16 March 1547.

He is rightly regarded as the restorer of Hebrew scholarship in France, and his Paris lectures drew large audiences, even Jews among them, yet he published nothing in his lifetime. From notes taken by his pupils Robert Estienne drew scholia for his edition of Leo of Juda's new Latin Bible. But Zurich Protestants shamefully garbled those notes, the Sorbonne condemned their Lutheran tendencies, and Vatable himself disowned them, though they remain a model of clear scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galle:
Galle, a diocese in Ceylon created by Leo XIII in August 1893, covers the Southern and Sabaragamuwa provinces, some 4,000 square miles. Of about 900,000 people, only 10,160 were Catholics in 1909, scattered among Sinhalese, Moors, and Tamils, Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Protestants. Racial and religious variety makes conversion and teaching slow work.

Leo XIII gave the new see to Belgian Jesuits, with Joseph Van Reeth as first bishop, consecrated at Antwerp in March 1895. He arrived with three priests and a lay brother that November. Progress ran slow but steady: confessions rose from 6,381 in 1897 to 27,956 in 1908, schools grew from fourteen to thirty-nine, and Saint Aloysius College opened in 1901. Sisters' lace even won gold at Saint Louis in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genealogy-in-:
Genealogy in the Bible treats the lists that open with the words these are the generations, a phrase the article reads as simply this is the history. The word genealogy itself appears only twice in the New Testament and rarely in the Old, yet lists crowd the early books. Primitive history, the entry argues, was genealogy dressed with anecdotes.

The article first untangles the heading, noting that heaven and earth have no posterity and that the Flood story follows the formula in Genesis. It then names the chief lists: Adam to Noah, Noah's sons as peoples, Shem to Abraham, Thare's line, Nahor's, Ishmael's, Jacob's sons, Esau's princes, and Jacob's house entering Egypt. Sources, weight, and gaps of each list follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-d:
Geoffrey of Dunstable, also called Geoffrey of Gorham, ruled Saint Albans Abbey wisely for twenty-six years. A scholar from Maine in Normandy, he was invited to lead the abbey school, found the post filled on arrival, and opened his own school at Dunstable instead. After borrowing copes for a miracle play, he lost house and all in a fire the night after the show.

To repay God and the saint for the copes, Geoffrey became a monk of Saint Albans, rose to prior, and was elected abbot in 1119. He built an infirmary with chapel and spent lavishly on a new shrine for Saint Alban's body, translated in August 1129. He endowed Sopwell nunnery, founded Markyate for Christina the recluse, and opened a leper hospital. He even saved the abbey in Stephen's civil war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-d-an:
Giuseppe D'Annibale was a cardinal and theologian born at Borbona in the diocese of Rieti on 22 September 1815, who died at the same place on 18 July 1892. He taught at the seminary of Rieti and later served as vicar-general of the diocese. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a moral theologian of two valued works.

Leo XIII made him titular Bishop of Caryste in 1881 and created him Cardinal-Priest of Saints Boniface and Alexis in 1889. He became Prefect of the Congregation of Indulgences. His treatise on moral theology, the Summula theologiae moralis, appeared at Milan from 1881 to 1883. His commentary on the constitution Apostolicae Sedis, published at Rieti in 1880, is also valued by theologians and canonists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gremiale:
Within Catholic ceremonial dress, the gremiale is a square or oblong cloth that a bishop wears over his lap while seated on his throne. The entry lists its moments of use: the choir's singing of the Kyrie, Gloria, and Credo, the giving out of blessed candles, palms, or ashes, and anointings at ordinations. It never appears at pontifical Vespers.

Its plain job is to keep other vestments, above all the chasuble, clean. Silk serves for pontifical Mass, marked with a central cross and silk embroidery in the chasuble's colour, while linen serves at other functions so it can be washed. First noted about 1311, it is not blessed and carries no symbolic meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grenoble:
Grenoble's entry covers a French diocese now made up of the Isère department and the canton of Villeurbanne, tracing its bishops from Domninus, present at Aquileia in 381, through reforming St. Hugh, restorer Pierre Scarron, and charity organizer Cardinal Le Camus. A second part treats the older Archbishopric of Vienne and the legends around its first bishops.

Monastic life fills much of the story, from early Benedictine and Augustinian priories to the Carthusians founded by St. Bruno in 1084, alongside the Waldenses, the wars of religion, and the passages of Popes Pius VI and Pius VII through the city. Readers get both a diocesan survey and a critical look at Vienne's forged early claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-del:
Paris mapmaker Guillaume Delisle, born in 1675, remade cartography by building maps on measured astronomy instead of copied guesswork. His father Claude taught geography and drew maps. The son's Map of the World and Map of the Continents of 1700, followed by maps of each land worked out one by one, set a new standard. It won him the new post of First Royal Geographer.

Delisle used French astronomers' scale measurements to fix places and sifted travel books and older maps where star readings ran short. He named his sources on disputed points and kept one fixed scale across neighbouring regions. The entry praises his corrected longitudes, full place lists, and careful spelling of names, and notes his Academy ranks from élève in 1702 to associé in 1718.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebrew-bible:
The Hebrew Bible holds the whole Old Testament except the seven deuterocanonical books and the added portions of Esther and Daniel. This Jewish tradition never counted in the official Hebrew canon. Protestant versions follow its contents, while its threefold shape, Law, Prophets, and Writings, predates the prologue to Ecclesiasticus and differs sharply from the Septuagint order taken up by the Vulgate.

Law gives the five books of Moses in fixed order. Prophets join Joshua through Kings with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve Minor Prophets as one book. Writings gather Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five festival Rolls, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles. Scribes first wrote bare consonants, then added word spacing, verse marks, and Massoretic helps, counting every letter, before Christian chapter numbers entered printed Hebrew Bibles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-seus:
Tyrolese Dominican Heinrich Seuse Denifle, born at Imst in 1844, was paleographer, historian, and Vatican archive keeper whose work reshaped the study of mystic thought and medieval seats of learning. A village schoolmaster's son, he entered the Dominicans at Graz in 1861, taught philosophy and theology there for a decade, and preached apologetic sermons printed in 1872.

His harvest of 2,500 fourteenth-century mystical texts in 1873, his exposure of the Gottesfreund as a myth. His proof that Catholic mystic thought rests on scholastic theology made his name. As archive keeper from 1883 he hunted Thomas Aquinas manuscripts across Europe and wrote the first volume of a university history in 1885. It showed these schools did not generally grow from cathedral schools and at first often taught no theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-etienne:
Chemist Henri-Etienne Sainte-Claire Deville, born at St. Thomas in the West Indies in 1818, made aluminium a commercial metal and discovered dissociation. After eight years in a self-built Paris laboratory without teachers or pupils, he organized Besançon's science faculty in 1844. He taught at the École Normale from 1851 and succeeded Dumas at the Sorbonne in 1859.

His mineral chemistry ranks him among the century's great chemists. Dissociation from 1857, nitrogen pentoxide, and a sodium process for aluminium, first found by Wöhler in 1827, let Napoleon III admire the silver of clay. With Debray he worked platinum metallurgy and pushed petroleum and heavy oils as steam fuel, publishing widely in the Comptes rendus and Annales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-chichel:
Henry Chichele, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1414, rose from a yeoman's family at Higham Ferrers through Winchester College and New College, Oxford, to many livings and legal offices. A skilled canon lawyer, he served Henry IV on missions to popes and to the King of France, attended the Council of Pisa, and was consecrated Bishop of St. David's in 1408 before the king nominated him to Canterbury. There he became Henry V's trusted councillor.

Chichele pursued the Lollards vigorously and defended ecclesiastical liberties against the statutes of Provisors and Praemunire. Martin V twice passed him over for the cardinalate and suspended his legatine office for weakness in pressing repeal. His lasting monuments are charitable and academic: a college and hospital at Higham Ferrers, and at Oxford the College of All Souls, whose modern history chair still bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-cole:
Henry Cole, a confessor of the faith born about 1500, studied at Winchester and New College, Oxford. There he became a perpetual fellow in 1523, then spent seven years in Italy, chiefly at Padua. He accumulated preferments, including the wardenship of New College, before returning to the Catholic faith about 1547 and resigning them all. Under Mary he rose again as Archdeacon of Ely, canon of Westminster, vicar-general to Cardinal Pole, and debater against Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer at Oxford.

Elizabeth's reign brought the reverse: fined 500 marks, deprived of every preferment, committed to the Tower in May 1560 and then to the Fleet. There he remained nearly twenty years until his death in 1579 or 1580. Cole's writings survive largely inside other men's books. Disputations and sermons printed in Foxe's Acts and Monuments, answers to Protestant propositions in Burnet, and letters from Padua and Paris all trace a scholar caught between two religious settlements.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hexham-and-ne:
Hexham and Newcastle is the English diocese whose roots run back to an abbey founded in 674 by St. Wilfrid of York on land Queen St. Etheldreda gave. When York's diocese was divided in 678, Hexham became a bishopric for the land between the Aln and the Tees. Of the eleven bishops who followed the first bishop, St. Eata, six were saints, including St. John of Beverley and St. Acca, to whom Bede dedicated several works.

The ancient line ended with Tidfert about 821. Danish devastation brought disorder until Hexham monastery rose again in 1113 as a priory of Austin Canons, flourishing until its dissolution under Henry VIII. The bishopric meanwhile merged into Lindisfarne, removed to Chester-le-Street and then to Durham. The entry carries the story from those early saints through the priory years to the modern diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-carb:
Ignatius Carbonnelle was a Belgian professor of mathematics and science, born at Tournai in 1829 and dead at Brussels in 1889. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1844, gave himself to mathematical study, and contributed papers to the Royal Academy of Belgium's bulletins. After ordination, Calcutta claimed six years of his teaching, 1861 to 1867.

At Calcutta he became first editor of the Indo-European Correspondence from 1865 to 1867. Returning to Europe, he taught mathematics and astronomy at Louvain, then joined the staffs of Études, the Revue Catholique, and Brussels scientific annals and reviews. The Scientific Society of Brussels dates to his founding in 1875; he served as its secretary from 1877 and edited its annals and review until his death. Some essays were reprinted as Les Confins de la Science et de la Philosophie.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inspiration-o:
Four questions drive this theology entry. Why do Catholics hold that certain books carry God's word? What does that inspiration mean? How far does it reach? How do Protestant views differ? Belief in sacred books runs as old as Hebrew literature itself, the entry notes. Moses and the prophets wrote down part of the message they were sent to deliver to Israel.

Prophets counted as authorized speakers of God's thoughts and wishes. They were called men of God and men of the Spirit. After the exile, the Temple and the Book anchored the people's religious and national renewal. Philo, writing around the turn of the era, already spoke of sacred books and most holy scripture. The entry builds from that Jewish ground toward the Catholic doctrine and its Protestant critics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-and-j:
Jacques de Lamberville was a Jesuit missionary born at Rouen in 1641. He died at Quebec in 1710. He joined the Society in 1661. He sailed to Canada in 1675. He labored almost without break on the Iroquois missions until death. At Onondaga he recognized a saint's soul in the Algonquin captive Catherine Tegakwitha. He instructed and baptized her.

He helped his brother Jean pacify Iroquois angered by Governor de la Barre's ill-timed campaign. After respite at Quebec and Montreal, he returned to Onondaga at native request. He left in 1709 through Abraham Schuyler's intrigues. He lived among the Iroquois while French and English rivalry for their alliance endangered missioners' lives. Charlevoix called him one of New France's holiest missionaries. The Indians called him the divine man. Jean's parallel career frames the same frontier story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-delil:
French abbé and man of letters Jacques Delille was born at Aigueperse on 22 June 1738. He died at Paris on 1 May 1813. He was educated at Paris' Collège de Lisieux. He became an instructor at the Collège de la Marche in Paris. His verse translation of Virgil's Georgics appeared in 1770. It won very great success and later gained him a seat in the French Academy.

He was then named to the poetry chair at the Collège de France. Through Count d'Artois' patronage he received the abbey of Saint-Séverin as a benefice, though he took only minor orders. In 1786 he accompanied Count de Choiseul to Constantinople and visited Greece. The Revolution stripped him of post and benefice. In 1794 he left France for exile in Switzerland, Germany, and England. He later returned to France. The entry follows a fashionable verse translator through revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-warren-:
Irish bishop James Warren Doyle was born near New Ross, County Wexford, in 1786. He died at Carlow in 1834. He belonged to a respectable but poor family. He was educated at Clonleigh, Rathconrogue, and later at New Ross' Augustinian college. Shortly after 1800 he joined the Augustinian order and was sent to Coimbra, Portugal. There at university he first showed great intellectual powers. In the university library he read everything, Voltaire and Rousseau among others.

As a consequence his faith became unsettled, but his vigorous intellect soon reasserted itself. Afterwards he became a fearless champion of the Church of his birth. During the French invasion he did sentry duty at Coimbra and accompanied the English to Lisbon as interpreter. He so impressed the Portuguese court that high employment was offered him. He declined it and returned to Ireland. The entry presents a bishop famed as Ireland's fearless controversialist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Corneille, a French painter and engraver born in Paris about 1646 and dead there in 1695, learned his craft from his father Michel. Called the younger Corneille, he took academy prizes in 1664 and 1668, studied in Rome, and entered the Royal Academy in 1675 with a scene of Hercules punishing Busiris.

Corneille painted for Paris churches, Notre-Dame, and the Tuileries, and became academy professor in 1692. His manner followed the Desiderosi school, a touch below his brother Michel in design and drawing. He also etched plates after his own pictures and after the Carracci, with a spirited hand that showed full command of line and acid.

Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, sieur de Bienville, Louisiana's French governor and the founder of New Orleans, was born at Montreal in 1680 and died in Paris in 1767. His father settled in Canada in 1640, and his brothers Iberville, Sérigny, and Chateauguay all helped shape early Louisiana.

Sailing with Iberville in 1698, Bienville helped found Biloxi, became its commandant in 1700, and governor after his brother's death in 1706. He fought the Natchez, finished Fort Rosalie, and under shifting companies held the colony through lean years. His lasting act came in 1718, when he laid out New Orleans, the city that grew into Louisiana's heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-chapeauv:
Jean Chapeauville, a Belgian theologian and historian born at Liège in 1551 and dead there in 1617, served his city church for a lifetime. After philosophy at Cologne and Louvain and a theology licentiate, he became synodal examiner in 1578, parish priest of Saint Michael's in 1579, and later provost of Saint Peter's.

Chapeauville also held posts as penitentiary canon, archdeacon of Famenne, inquisitor, and vicar-general under two bishops of Liège. He won praise for nursing the sick in the 1581 plague, for piety, and for teaching theology in Liège monasteries. He pressed Trent's reforms at home, above all a clerical seminary and open contests for parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-haute:
Jean de Hautefeuille, a French physicist born at Orléans in 1647 and dead there in 1724. He was a baker's son lifted by the Duchess of Bouillon, who funded his studies, took him through England and Italy, and left him a pension. Entering the Church, he held benefices from her gift.

Hautefeuille turned an inventive mind to clocks, proposing a coiled spring and balance wheel to replace the pendulum, a notion Huygens and Hooke also claimed. He studied speaking trumpets and echoes, improved lenses, sought to lift water by gunpowder blasts, and built a tide gauge he called a thalassameter. Genius he had, but rarely the patience to finish what he began.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-mande:
Jean de Mandeville, supposed author of a medieval book of travels much read in his age, is said to have died in 1372. The writer calls himself an English knight born at Saint Albans who left in 1322. He fought as a mercenary in Egypt, crossed Palestine, India, inner Asia, and China, and served the Great Khan for fifteen months.

After thirty-four years abroad he returned in 1356 and, with a physician met in Egypt, wrote his account at Liège. Later study showed the true author was Jean de Bourgoigne, a Liège physician who had seen only Egypt and stitched his book from other travellers' tales. Its wide reading and lively telling still made it a medieval bestseller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-paul-med:
Jean-Paul Médaille, a French Jesuit missionary born at Carcassonne in 1618 and dead at Auch in 1689. He joined the Society in 1640, taught college courses for years, including six years of philosophy, and then preached for eighteen years as his life's work.

Formed in the school of Saint Francis Régis, Médaille evangelised Velay, Auvergne, Languedoc, and Aveyron, founding fervent sodalities of men and women wherever he preached. Those groups taught children, visited the sick, and aided the poor, carrying his missions' fruits onward. Age and austerity at last turned him to directing sodalities and hearing confessions, above all of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-sire-de-:
Jean, Sire de Joinville, seneschal of Champagne and historian, was born in 1225 and died at Joinville in 1317. His family held high feudal rank in Champagne, and his father Simon defended Troyes in 1230 before dying in 1233, leaving Jean to his mother Beatrix of Burgundy.

Joinville took the cross in 1248, following Saint Louis yet refusing the king's oath since he was not his man. Funding two bannerets and ten knights himself, he sailed from Marseilles, joined Louis at Cyprus, fought in Egypt. He faced grave danger at Mansourah in 1250, fell ill, and was captured with the king. Freed that May, he followed Louis to Acre and later wrote the life of the saint-king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk Schelble was a German musician remembered as the founder of Frankfurt's Society of St. Cecilia. Born in the Black Forest in 1789, he sang at the Stuttgart court and opera, studied composition there, and went to Vienna in 1814, where he met Beethoven. In 1818 he became first tenor at Frankfurt, the city where he spent the rest of his life.

Starting with weekly musical evenings in his own house, Schelble built the Cacilienverein from twenty-one members in 1818 to about a hundred within a few years. Its concerts brought Mozart, Handel, Haydn, Beethoven, and after 1828 Bach to Frankfurt audiences, alongside older masters such as Palestrina. When illness forced him home in 1836, Felix Mendelssohn took his place, and friends praised Schelble's character as warmly as his art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-c-drumgo:
John C. Drumgoole was an Irish-born priest whose Mission of the Immaculate Virgin sheltered thousands of homeless New York children. Born at Granard in 1816, he emigrated to New York in 1824, worked as a shoemaker to support his widowed mother, and became sexton of St. Mary's in 1844. Running a small bookshop to fund his studies, he entered the seminary in 1865 and was ordained in 1869.

Put in charge of a languishing boys' lodging-house of the St. Vincent de Paul Society, he revived it, founded St. Joseph's Union to support it worldwide, and in 1881 opened an imposing Mission building on Great Jones Street. A Staten Island farm, Mount Loretto, followed, with trade schools run by Franciscan sisters, housing two thousand destitute children a year. At his death in 1888 he left the whole enterprise free of debt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-constabl:
John Constable, writing as Clerophilus Alethes, was an English Jesuit controversialist who defended Catholic orders against Anglican claims. Born in Lincolnshire in 1676 or 1678, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1695. He served the Fitzherbert family at Swinnerton for many years, where he is buried.

His chief opponents were the Abbe Courayer, who championed Anglican ordinations after coming to England in 1728, and Charles Dodd, who wrote with prejudice against Jesuits. Constable answered Courayer's defense of English ordinations with remarks proving their invalidity. He mocked him as a sham defender writing only for booty. He wrote on the ancient doctrine of the Eucharist and on amendments to Dodd's Church History of England, dying in 1743.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-doyle:
John Doyle was an English portrait painter and caricaturist whose signed drawings, H.B., charted the politics of his age. Born in Dublin in 1797, he studied under Gabrielli and the miniature painter Comerford. He came to London in 1821 as a portrait painter and turned to caricature in 1827. He formed his signature from his initials, the letters J and D placed one above the other.

From 1829 to 1851 he produced a famous series of drawings in brilliant style on every political movement of the day. Unlike Rowlandson and Gillray, his work is marked by reticence, courtesy, and good breeding, clever and at times stinging in epigram, though Thackeray underrated it as merely genteel. Some six hundred drawings in the British Museum form a graphic history of England's politics. Doyle kept his incognito to the last, retiring seventeen years before his death in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-machale:
John MacHale was the Irish Archbishop of Tuam whose long life spanned the hedge schools, the Famine, and the struggle for Catholic freedom. Born at Tubbernavine in County Mayo in 1791, so feeble at birth that he was baptized at home, he ran barefoot to the hedge school. He listened to saints' lives, national songs, and tales of the French Revolution from his uncle, and watched French troops march to Castlebar in 1798.

At sixteen he won a bursarship to Maynooth, where emigre French priests taught him French, Latin, Greek, Italian, German, and Hebrew, plus the English classics. After seven years he was appointed lecturer in theology in 1814 while still a subdeacon. He was ordained at twenty-four and became professor in 1820. Students esteemed him for a zeal and earnestness that marked his whole career as priest, bishop, and champion of his people until his death in 1881.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-haute:
John of Hauteville was a twelfth-century moralist and satirical poet, author of the Latin poem Archithrenius. Little is known of his life: he was probably not English-born and not a Benedictine, and he flourished about 1184. His one certain work, eight cantos named for its hero, the Prince of Lamentations, follows the hero's search for a remedy for human woes.

In a prose prologue Archithrenius deplores men's miseries and sets out for Nature. He passes through Venus's palace, the land of belly-worshippers, and Paris. There a eulogy of the city contrasts with the wretchedness of its students, valuable evidence for the early university. He climbs the mountains of Ambition and Presumption and meets the monster Cupidity and the greed of prelates. He hears Greek sages declaim against vice at Thule, and at last finds Nature, who prescribes marriage with Moderation as his cure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-joseph-v:
Karl Joseph von Hefele was Bishop of Rottenburg, born at Unterkochen in Württemberg in 1809 and dead at Rottenburg in 1893. The son of a royal furnace superintendent, he studied at Ellwangen, Ehingen, and Tübingen, and was ordained in 1833. He succeeded Möhler in Tübingen's church history chair in 1836 and held it until his election as bishop in 1869. Following Möhler, he joined historical accuracy to a firm grasp of facts and a great power of exposition.

His lectures drew hundreds of students, and later manuals by Knöpfler and Funk rested on his teaching. Besides some 150 Kirchenlexikon articles, his standard work was the seven-volume Conciliengeschichte, reaching to the fifteenth century. At the Vatican Council he stood among the bishops opposing papal infallibility, publishing his reasons in Causa Honorii Papae and voting Non placet on 13 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-rochelle: A 1913 entry on La Rochelle — the Huguenot port. Georges Goyau unfolds its stormy past. The siege broke the Calvinist pride. France knew the fateful name. The seventeenth century told its tale. Its 1628 siege is famed. Its harbor is famed. Its 1628 royal siege is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-neale: This 1913 reference piece on Neale — the Archbishop of Baltimore. James McNeal honors his famous see. His rule steered the American Church. The flock bless the prudent name. The nineteenth century knew his sway. His 1817 death is famed. His 1815 Baltimore is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lille: A 1913 entry on Lille — the Flemish diocese. Georges Goyau gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the northern flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the French north. Its 1913 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed. Its 1913 industrial diocese is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-braille: This 1913 reference piece on Braille — the blind inventor. George Sauvage honors his famous dots. His art loosed the sightless reading. The world bless the patient name. The nineteenth century knew his gift. His 1852 death is famed. His 1829 dots are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louisville: A 1913 entry on Louisville — the Kentucky diocese. P.M.J. Rock gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the Ohio flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the American south. Its 1808 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maniple: This 1913 reference article on the Maniple — the Mass vestment. Joseph Braun unfolds its liturgical lore. It graces the priestly arm. The Church keeps the ancient use. The sacristies know its form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its festal form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuscripts-o: This 1913 reference piece on the Biblical Manuscripts — the text's witnesses. Walter Drum surveys their ancient lore. The codices guard the sacred words. The scholars mine their vellum pages. The libraries keep their fame. Their 1907 study is famed. Their vellum pages are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-marguer: A 1913 entry on d'Youville — the Grey Nuns' foundress. Lionel Lindsay honors her famous charity. Her zeal served the Montreal poor. Canada bless the holy name. The eighteenth century knew her toil. Her 1771 death is famed. Her 1737 sisters are famed. Her 1737 Montreal charity is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-masolino-da-p: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Masolino — the Brancacci painter. Louis Gillet honors his famous frescoes. His brush graced the Florentine chapel. Italy bless the gifted hand. The fifteenth century knew his art. His 1447 death is famed. His 1427 frescoes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miracle: This 1913 reference piece on Miracle — the wondrous sign. John T. Driscoll unfolds its theological lore. It seals the divine message. The theologians weigh the seemly bounds. The Church keeps its ancient teaching. Its 1907 study is famed. Its wondrous sign is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monreale: Monreale's cathedral blazes with Norman mosaics, the great Christ Pantocrator gazing down in gold. This entry covers its foundation by William II, its art, and its archdiocese. The most dazzling church of Norman Sicily, where 6,000 square meters of mosaic tell the Bible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-von-ab: Moritz von Aberle was the Tübingen theologian whose biblical scholarship bridged the old exegesis and the new criticism. This entry covers his career, his works, and his influence. A scholar between two ages: his exegesis honored tradition while welcoming new learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nashville: Nashville, the Athens of the South, built its Catholic life around the diocese founded in 1837. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and institutions. The faith in Music City: its cathedral and schools serve Tennessee's Catholics to this day, from the city to the countryside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neville: This entry profiles the Neville name in English Catholic history, tracing its notable bearers and their place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact family sketch from the encyclopedia's English gallery, preserved among its records of England's recusant houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newbattle: Newbattle was the great Cistercian abbey of the Scottish borders, founded by David I in 1140. This entry traces its history, its abbots, and its ruins. White monks in the borderlands: its ruins still dominate the Esk valley in the Scottish borders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oracle: Oracles were the pagan shrines where gods were thought to speak, from Delphi to Dodona. This entry surveys their history, their methods, and the Church's judgment. The voices of the old gods: the Fathers saw demons behind their mysterious utterances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-candl: The Paschal candle is the great Easter candle, the pillar of wax that proclaims Christ risen. This entry explains its symbolism, its blessing, and its history. The light of the resurrection, in wax: its flame burns through the fifty days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pectorale: The pectorale is the bishop's pectoral cross, worn over the heart as the sign of his office. This entry explains its form, its history, and its symbolism. The cross at the bishop's breast: its heavy golden chain marks his jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-photius-of-co: Photius was the brilliant patriarch whose quarrel with Rome opened the road to the Eastern schism. This long entry traces his career, his learning, and the controversy. The most learned man of the ninth century: his Bibliotheca preserved the classics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-andre-: Pierre-André Latreille was the priest-entomologist who saved natural history from the Revolution's prisons. This entry covers his career, his insects, and his fame. The prince of entomologists: his countless beetles filled the great Paris museum of natural history completely full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cornei: Corneille was the father of French tragedy, whose Cid and Horace ennobled the stage. This entry covers his career, his plays, and his fame. The Roman of the French theatre: his immortal Cid made the French stage heroic forever after.

charlotte-temple:
Susanna Rowson, billed as Mrs. Rowson, wrote Charlotte Temple, first published in London in 1791 and then in America, where it became the young nation's best-selling novel for decades. Charlotte is a schoolgirl of fifteen at a boarding school near London. A dashing officer, Montraville, charms her with the help of a scheming teacher, and talks her into sailing with him to America, promising marriage he never performs.

In New York she is kept, then cast off when he tires and marries money. Pregnant, poor, and ill, she is turned away by his new household and dies after giving birth, begging her father's pardon. Rowson frames the tale as a warning to young women and their parents, and readers wept over it for a century.

The contents follow the Colonel's house in Bedford Place and his garden spot of Virginia seeking an outlet to the sea. They also cover the arrival of a true Southern lady, important letters, and the Colonel's schemes to recover his fortunes. Chad dishing the dinner, the old clock tower and the Colonel's office give the tales their flavour. Readers who enjoy post-war Southern humour, told with affection for old Virginia manners, will find the Colonel delightful company.

Seven chapters follow the Empress Dowager from early life through training, rule, reaction, and reform. Other chapters treat the Emperor Kuang Hsu, Prince Chun the regent, court ladies, and princesses. Headland had unusual access and photographs from court circles. The book preserves a close view of the Qing court in its final years before 1911.

Mr Crotchet, a city millionaire, hosts and provokes them.

Miss Touchandgo's vanished fortune nips one love affair in the bud, she losing a fortune as well as a lover, while songs, dinners, and a threatened riot fill the talk. Peacock's method is dialogue as fencing. Crotchet Castle, many think his best novel, skewers the steam intellect of 1831 with unmatched lightness.

dora-deane-or-the-east-india-uncle:
Dora Deane, or The East India Uncle, by Mary Jane Holmes, opens beside a deathbed in a third story room. Morning sun falls on a face worn thin by suffering. Dora is about to lose her mother, an invalid on a low, scanty bed. The girl is to be left to an uncle in India, her father's brother. Strange relatives and a sea voyage wait past the grief.

Louise Mühlbach's Empress Josephine, translated from the German by the Reverend W. Binet, follows the Creole viscountess from Martinique to the throne of France. Book One is the Viscountess Beauharnais: the young maid, the betrothal, the unhappy marriage, and the Revolution. Her arrest, prison, and deliverance close it; her husband went to the guillotine, and she nearly followed. Book Two makes her the wife of General Bonaparte: Toulon, the 13th Vendémiaire, and the first interview.

Inside, Bonaparte's love-letters from Italy burn beside Josephine's Parisian debts and dangers. Mühlbach writes her as the Revolution's survivor turned empress of manners, softening a conqueror's court. Readers get the romantic German school of Napoleonic biography at its most readable. Documented scenes and invented conversations carry a heroine whose charm counts, as contemporaries counted it, as a political force.
essays-in-little:
Andrew Lang's Essays in Little, published by Henry and Co in 1891 with his portrait, collects short critical pieces, five of them new for the volume. The contents range over Alexandre Dumas, Stevenson's works, Thackeray, Dickens, Homer and the study of Greek, the sagas, and John Bunyan. A letter to a young journalist and a paper on Kipling's stories close the book.

Lang writes as a friendly guide rather than a hanging judge, praising buccaneer adventures and Scott's poems in the same breath. A duel scene with Captain John Barry doffing his kepi shows his taste for gallant romance. These little essays trained a generation's reading habits, and their ease still conceals how much Lang actually knew.

govdocs-archive_org-principles-of-counte: Chapter 5 of a work on counterdeception takes up deception in the global security environment. It lays out rules for counterdeception: how to spot lies told by rival states and how to answer them. Deception is an old tool of war and diplomacy, and the chapter treats it as a problem with methods, not mysteries. The author is not named in the record. Strategists and students of intelligence are its natural readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Long before the missiles arrived, Cuba spent two years asking Moscow for arms and protection. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, posted in November 2022 for the sixtieth anniversary of the Cuban Missile Crisis. It is the second part of a series on getting to know the Cubans.

From late 1960 into early 1961, Cuban-Soviet ties grew stronger month by month. Cuban leaders repeatedly requested military help and security guarantees from the Soviets. They voiced rising fear of an American attack. The records correct a common habit of telling 1962 as only a Washington-Moscow story.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cuba_A_Harsh_and_:
At the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, Fidel Castro wrote to Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev. He urged a course so extreme that the letter is still known by a grim label: the Armageddon letter. A National Security Archive news post from January 2018 presents that letter and the harsh and terrible solution it proposed.

Castro feared an American attack on Cuba was near, and his letter pushed Khrushchev toward striking first rather than waiting. Khrushchev refused, and the crisis ended with Soviet missiles withdrawn instead. Few single documents show the pressure leaders put on each other in those thirteen days so starkly. The posting gives readers the text's meaning in context: an ally's panic, a superpower's restraint, and how close the arguments came to the worst outcome.
green-short-history-english-people:
Green's Short History of the English People, in the 1883 printing, retold the national past for a vast public. Chaucer and the plowman share his stage with kings and queens. Social life comes first, where older histories put battles and courts alone.

The book sold in the hundreds of thousands and changed its trade. Green made history a story of the people's work, faith, and song. His vivid sketches of towns, fields, and workshops won readers everywhere. Critics praised its freshness while scholars used it for decades. It stands as the Victorian classic that opened English history to common readers.
greenmantle: Greenmantle, John Buchan's thriller. Another edition. This book preserves that novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
hawthorne-and-his-circle:
Julian Hawthorne's Hawthorne and His Circle is a son's informal memoir of Nathaniel Hawthorne and the friends around him. Julian calls his father the central figure, and treats his own good fortune in inheriting such friendships as both privilege and difficulty.

Contents move from dates, his aunt Lizzie's efforts and his mother's strong-box to the spirit of The Scarlet Letter, the strain of imaginative composition, and the house on Mall Street. The haunted mahogany writing-desk, the flowered writing-gown, scarlet fever and children's plays fill the early chapters. Readers of American literature will find Julian's lights and shadows of memory intimate, gossipy and revealing.
his-own-people:
Booth Tarkington opened His Own People in the palm-room of a grand Rome hotel. A young American poet watches high society at tea there. He whispers that he has come unto his own people at last. Mellin has dreamed since schooldays of the beau monde, the fashionable world, and Rome seems to hand it to him. Glamorous new friends take him up, admire his verses, and draw him into their circle.

Tarkington lets the shine curdle: the circle lives by cards and credit, and the poet's money and innocence are the real attraction. Fleeced and sobered, Mellin learns where his own people actually are. The novel is a comedy of snobbery with a sting, written in Tarkington's polished early manner.
imperial-purple:
Edgar Saltus's Imperial Purple paints the Caesars in the colors of decay. The contents promise the program: That Woman, Conjectural Rome, Fabulous Fields, The Pursuit of the Impossible, Nero, The House of Flavia, The Poison in the Purple, Faustine, and The Agony. It opens with Caesar's murder done and the heralds shouting. Saltus lingers on the conqueror famous for giving away fortunes while dining on dry bread. Rome's greatness and Rome's rot are the same subject here.

Inside, emperors and empresses pass in a pageant of luxury and cruelty. Saltus writes history as the decadents read it: for the perfume and the poison. His sources are the scandalous ones, Suetonius above all. Readers get the 1890s American decadence in prose form, a book to be savored sentence by sentence rather than believed.
j-cole:
Emma Gellibrand's J. Cole is a comic story told through the misspelled letter of a boy seeking a place as page. J. Cole writes that he is over thirteen, can clean plate, wait at table, clean windows and boots, and add figures, and that his brother, under a butler, taught him.

His letter, enclosed in a clumsy home-made envelope and written in a large hand with blots and smears, asks eight shillings and all found, or seven if his washing is done. The narrator, who advertised for a page-boy and puzzled through dozens of answers, reaches Cole's last. Readers who enjoy Victorian humour in dialect spelling will find J. Cole brief and charming.
jane-cable:
Jane Cable, by George Barr McCutcheon, is a Chicago romance built on a foundling's secret. McCutcheon's contents name the pieces in order: the Cables, James Bansemer, the foundling, and the Bansemer crash. Jane, raised in comfort, grows up near a truth about her birth that other people guard, trade on, and fear, while young Bansemer rises through the wreck of his father's fortunes.

In Sight of the Fangs and The Canker darken the middle chapters, and a tragedy at the sea wall brings hours of terror. David Cable's debts and a second crash pull father and son into the open at last. The final chapter moves to the Philippines, where the American empire gives the story its closing stage. Birth, money, and reputation are the three currencies here, and McCutcheon spends the first two freely to test the third.
leonie-of-the-jungle:
Joan Conquest published her novel Leonie of the Jungle in New York in 1921. She had earlier written Desert Love. The Macaulay Company held the copyright that year.

Conquest dedicated the book to a native of India she calls splendid. Two books divide the tale: The West and The East. An epigraph quotes the line that East and West never meet. Leonie's story tests that claim through love and danger. Jungle settings and colonial romance drive Conquest's popular plot. Kipling's famous line frames her East-West romance. Conquest wrote many such colonial love stories for eager readers.
life-s-handicap-being-stories-of-mine-ow:
Rudyard Kipling gathers these stories of his own people in India. A 1915 printing carries his dedication dating the tales to 1887 and 1889. The preface describes a monastery called the Chubara of Dhunni Bhagat. Worn-out priests meditated in its gaily painted brick cells there.

Mango clumps, pipal trees, and tame parrots fill the courtyard. Hindu, Sikh, and Mahomedan mendicants rested together under its trees. One-eyed Gobind, a holy man, told Kipling the framing tale. Old men there found all creeds wonderfully alike and colourless. Parrots tore through the mango trees above brick-paved paths. Thousands of naked feet had worn those paths into gutters.
little-prudy-s-dotty-dimple:
Sophie May opens this children's book with Dotty's babyhood. Alice is the youngest of the Parlin family, readers learn. Grandma Read gathers the children into the kitchen. She tells them about their new little sister there.

Susy dances for joy at the news. Prudy falls down the cellar stairs in her delight. She rolls as softly as a pincushion, unhurt. Chapters promise verses, nestlings, parties, and a wedding to come. The bone man and Dotty's verses follow the babyhood chapter. Buying a brother and a wedding close her adventures. Fanny Harlow's party gives Dotty a social world beyond the nursery.
lord-arthur-savile:
Oscar Wilde made this set of short tales in 1891, in the same rich years as Dorian Gray. The title tale stands first, and three more tales stand by its side. Wilde's wit, so sharp in his plays, runs all through these prose tales too.

Lord Arthur Savile is told by a hand reader that he is fated to kill a man. In good faith, he sets out to get the deed done before his wedding day can come. 'The Canterville Ghost' turns the haunted house tale on its head, to great comic effect.
love-instigated-the-story-of-a-carved-iv:
Love Instigated is a slight gift-book tale by Douglass Sherley of Louisville, Kentucky. Its full title calls it the story of a carved ivory umbrella handle. The book was sold as a Christmas booklet in a box for one dollar. A de luxe edition, signed and limited to ninety-nine copies, cost ten.

Sherley also wrote The Story of a Picture, the adverts say. A companion tale, Love Perpetuated, tells the story of a dagger. The motto claims that the man who plants cabbages imitates God. Such dainty booklets were holiday gifts in the Gilded Age. This one survives as a curious piece of Louisville publishing.
lucile:
Lucile is a long verse novel by Owen Meredith, pen name of Edward Robert Bulwer Lytton. He dedicated the poem to his father, the famous novelist. A line from Hamlet stands at its head, about watching and sleeping. Meredith feared his new verse form had no footprints before it.

The poem tells of Lucile, a French lady of grace and sorrow. Two men love her, and her heart is torn between them. The tale moves through drawing rooms and across Europe's great events. Its smooth stanzas carried the story to a huge public. Lucile was the best-selling poem-novel of the Victorian age. Readers memorized its lines as they now memorize songs.
lulu-alice-and-jimmie-wibblewobble:
Lulu, Alice and Jimmie Wibblewobble is a children's book by Howard R. Garis. R. F. Fenno published it in New York in 1912, with colored pictures. It belongs to Garis's Bedtime Stories series for the very young. The Wibblewobbles are a family of ducks in his animal world.

Lulu and Alice are the sisters, and Jimmie is their brother. Short tales follow their small adventures, mishaps, and lessons. Garis wrote dozens of such animal books for children. His style is simple, warm, and full of gentle fun. The Wibblewobble stories sit beside his Littletail rabbit tales. They make easy reading for bedtime or first readers.
luther-bondage-of-the-will-cole:
Erasmus defended free will; Luther answered with The Bondage of the Will, the most uncompromising book he ever wrote. Henry Cole's English translation of 1823 carries the argument here. Luther himself ranked the treatise as his finest work, and scholars have argued about it ever since.

Human will, he claims, rides like a beast between God and Satan, unable to choose its rider. Only grace frees the captive will; nothing in us earns the rescue. The prose hits like a hammer, wit and fury mixed. Across the page stands Europe's greatest humanist, outmatched in sheer theological force. The debate over freedom and grace has never found a louder opening round.
mary-anerley-a-yorkshire-tale:
R. D. Blackmore published Mary Anerley, a Yorkshire tale, in 1880. The book opens far from any house, on a dreary moor road. That road drops to a swift river at Seven Corpse Ford.

Eight farmers once rode into that ford in fog and heavy rain. Seven drowned, and the place kept its grim name. Richard Yordas set stones and a chain there so their sons might cross safe, and worse news soon came. The Tees runs fast and can kill, Blackmore warns at length. Moor, ford, and hall give the tale its stark Yorkshire ground.
medieval-people:
Eileen Power wrote Medieval People, first printed in 1924. Power taught history at the University of London and at Girton College. Her preface defends a close, personal way of writing social history.

She says past lives live best when shown through one person at a time. As much proof can survive for a plain man as for a duke, she argues. Cloister and school, in a Langland quote, frame her world. The book rebuilds plain lives from records most histories pass by. Langland's Piers Plowman gives the book its front quote. Power's aim is the past made to live for plain readers.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
The Duke of Saint-Simon's memoirs appear here in a complete set. Fifteen volumes make up the whole work, by the contents list. Volume one opens with his birth, family, and early life.

He joins the Musketeers and marches to the siege of Namur. Dreadful weather, monks, and rival couriers fill that first campaign. Later heads treat the Duc de Chartres' wedding and the death of his father. The whole sweep runs from Louis XIV's court into the Regency years. Saint-Simon's eye for rank and slight fills each of the volumes. Few court lives of that age are told at such length.
memoirs-vieux-souvenirs-of-the-prince-de:
The Prince de Joinville's memoirs, Vieux Souvenirs, appear here in Lady Mary Loyd's English. Chapter one covers the years 1818 to 1830 of his life. He was born at Neuilly-sur-Seine on August 14, 1818.

A wet nurse took him at birth, as was the custom then. His first clear memory is a Twelfth Night dinner in 1824. Louis XVIII hosted the whole royal house at the Tuileries that night. Drums, guards, and the King's dinner passing on the stairs dazzled the boy. Talma on stage, in a gilt cuirass, struck the small boy too. A prince's childhood is shown through family rooms, not state halls.
moby-dick-or-the-whale:
Herman Melville published Moby-Dick at New York and London in 1851. He inscribed it to Nathaniel Hawthorne, in token of his admiration for Hawthorne's genius. The contents begin with Loomings, The Carpet Bag, and The Spouter-Inn. Ishmael, the narrator, signs aboard a Nantucket whaler after chapters on the town and its chowder.

Captain Ahab drives the Pequod after one white whale, Moby Dick. Melville mixes the hunt with whaling lore, sermons, and metaphysics. The book sold poorly in his lifetime and was rediscovered in the twentieth century. It now stands as the great American novel of obsession, labor, and the sea.
monitress-merle:
Angela Brazil wrote this girls' school story as a sequel by request. She dedicates it to readers who asked for the further adventures of Mavis and Merle. Treyer Evans illustrated the volume. The contents open with a last bathe and a school ballot. Merle becomes the new monitress of her school at Chagmouth.

The seaside setting brings fishermaidens, a ferry, and a boat called The Kittiwake. School episodes include the mumps, a performance facing the footlights, and fifth form justice. A haunted tree and Yuletide close the list. Brazil practically invented the modern school story, and her boarding-school world runs on friendship, scrapes, and honor.
mr-bingle:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote this novel, illustrated by James Montgomery Flagg. McCutcheon was known for Graustark and The Prince of Graustark. The contents open with the five little Sykeses and an odd relation. The death of Uncle Joe follows, and the story of Joseph. Thomas Singleton Bingle earns the title Honorable midway through.

Later chapters treat the affairs of Amy and Dick, and Mr. Bingle thinking of becoming an angel. Trouble triples, the law speaks its last word, and December brings another Christmas Eve. The opening scene warms the Bingle apartment in lower New York with a coal fire, since the steam pipes refuse to heat.
my-beautiful-lady-nelly-dale:
Thomas Woolner, a noted sculptor, wrote this tale in verse and prose. Cassell issued the 1887 edition in London, Paris, and New York. Its heroine is Nelly Dale, the beautiful lady of the title. An introduction praises Woolner's song of noble earthly love.

The intro frames love as a spur to high endeavor. Duty speaks like a call to war in its lines. The book joins a library built on belief in human worth. Milton is quoted on books that hold a potency of life. Woolner's tale is earnest Victorian romance, aiming to lift hearts by showing love that makes men strive.
my-neighbors-stories-of-the-welsh-people:
Caradoc Evans tells stories of the Welsh people in this 1920 book. Harcourt, Brace and Howe issued it in New York. Evans dedicated it to Thomas Burke of Limehouse Nights. An opening essay, The Welsh People, sets the tone.

He calls God a big man, taller than the highest chapel. Tales named Love and Hate and The Two Apostles follow. Treasure, widows, and unanswered prayers fill the contents. Evans writes of chapel folk with a hard, comic edge. His Welsh neighbors scheme, pray, and grasp in small villages. The book shocked some readers and made Evans the bold voice of Welsh fiction.
my-tropic-isle:
E. J. Banfield, famed as the beachcomber of Dunk Island, wrote this island book. Fisher Unwin issued it in London in 1911. Much of it first ran in the North Queensland Register as Rural Homilies. Banfield thanks museum men in Sydney for help naming specimens.

Two lines from Milton front the book, praising the wilderness. Banfield lived simply on a Great Barrier Reef isle. He writes of birds, reefs, weather, and his Aboriginal neighbors. V1 calls the result gentle natural history and an Australian classic. Turtles, shells, and bright birds fill a calm record of a man who chose the tropic shore.
nasa-tm-19630002674-cold-air-investigati:
John E. McAulay of Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-42, in September 1959. It reports cold-air tests of three rocket nozzles. Each nozzle can change the size of its throat, the narrow waist of the nozzle. The shape is called convergent-divergent, since it squeezes then flares.

Changing the throat lets a crew throttle thrust up or down. Cold flow tests use plain air, not hot exhaust, for safety and ease. McAulay measured how each design behaved across its range. Such data guided nozzles for engines that must vary their push, a key need for advanced rockets and jets.
nasa-tm-19650012052-ibm-7094-program-for:
Henry Miller at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this program description for the IBM 7094 computer. The program solves what the title calls the six-coil problem. It was written in Fortran, the standard language for scientific computing at the time. Goddard document X-543-64-366 covers the program.

Miller sets out what the program does and how it is organized. Program descriptions let other users run and trust a code without reading every line. They also let later staff maintain it. In 1964, a shared program like this one saved each new user from starting over.
nasa-tm-19680017759-are-gas-core-nuclear:
Robert G. Ragsdale of Lewis Research Center asks whether gas-core nuclear rockets can actually be built in this 1968 conference paper. In such an engine, gaseous nuclear fuel sits at the center of a cavity. Hydrogen propellant flows around the fuel and carries away fission heat as thermal radiation.

Ragsdale reduces engine needs to two key parameters. One is the share of cavity volume filled by gaseous fuel. The other is the ratio of hydrogen flow to uranium flow through the engine. He builds an engine performance map from those two values. Available experimental data are then placed on the map. The map lets engineers judge this concept against rivals fairly.
nasa-tm-19680026660-performance-of-a-col:
Robert A. Wasko and Douglas E. Harrington of Lewis Research Center tested a collapsible plug nozzle with two shroud designs in this 1968 report. One shroud was a two-position cylindrical type. The other was a variable angle floating shroud. Tests ran from rest up to Mach 2.0 flight conditions.

At subsonic cruise, both shrouds performed nearly the same. The two-position shroud did better during subsonic acceleration. The floating shroud did better at supersonic Mach numbers. External flow effects peaked at Mach 1.2 for both configurations. Static performance was measured across a wide range of nozzle pressure ratios. The study guides shroud choice for plug nozzle engines.
nasa-tm-19710002949-us-patents-for-nasa-:
NASA issued this catalog of United States patents for its own inventions. The patents listed are open for licensing inside the United States. Several thousand inventions, the introduction notes, result each year from NASA-supported research, covering nearly every field of technology, and many carry real commercial value.

Inventions with government importance or strong commercial promise are the ones NASA patents. To spread their use, the agency offers nonexclusive, royalty-free licenses for the life of a patent. If no commercial use appears within two years, an exclusive license may go to a qualified applicant instead. The catalog gives the application steps and the Washington office where inquiries were to be sent.
nasa-tm-19710009153-nuclear-power-for-su:
Frank E Rom of the Lewis Research Center wrote this technical paper on nuclear power for giant surface effect vehicles and aircraft. Rom presented early results from a cost study of very large nuclear craft built to haul cargo across oceans. Surface effect vehicles ride on a cushion of air just above the water.

The study found such craft might move cargo for one to two cents per ton mile. Moving all cargo worth shipping at that rate would take about fifteen hundred huge surface craft, or five hundred huge aircraft. Rom also reported reactor impact tests. Test reactors survived hits at high speed against reinforced concrete without leaking.
nasa-tm-19710011714-preliminary-results-:
Martin U Gutstein of the Lewis Research Center and James A Bond of General Electric reported these boiler tests in March 1971. The hardware was a single tube potassium boiler for the advanced Rankine system. That system was a planned nuclear electric power plant for space. Lithium heated the tube, and potassium boiled inside it.

Exit steam heat reached as high as fourteen hundred twenty kelvin. The report gives the heat pattern inside the boiler. It also gives pressure losses at varied potassium flow rates. Boiling heat transfer values cover a range of exit dryness and superheat. One test mimicked plant startup. The team called the test success a major step for hot liquid metal power systems.
nasa-tm-19710019491-compact-30-kw-circul:
G. E. McDonald, H. A. Putre, M. C. Swanson, and P. M. Finnegan of the Lewis Research Center wrote this memorandum, NASA TM X-52676, with L. Homyak of the Plum Brook Station. It describes a compact capsule that circulates helium to cool nuclear fuel specimens during tests. The capsule was built for work inside the NASA Plum Brook Reactor.

One capsule was endurance tested outside the reactor, and two more were run inside it. The abstract lists demonstrated performance: high pressures, wall temperatures, and specimen powers up to the capsule's thirty-kilowatt rating. The design uses a motor-driven vane pump, a concentric tube heat exchanger, and a fuel test section made from modified commercial parts. The authors note that a loss-of-coolant accident could be contained without shutting the reactor down, and that spent capsules are cheap enough to discard.
nasa-tm-19720013351-peak-axial-velocity-:
D E Groesbeck, U H von Glahn, and R G Huff of the Lewis Research Center studied jet noise in March 1972, as NASA TM X-68047. Their concern was the externally blown flap, a lift system for short takeoff aircraft. Engine jets strike the lowered flaps and gain lift. That striking also creates an unacceptable rise in noise. Lowering the jet speed before impact is the known cure.

The speed must fall within a set distance behind the nozzle. Multi element nozzles promise that faster decay of peak jet speed. The team compared rectangular and triangular nozzle shapes for the job. Their measurements tracked how fast the centerline velocity dropped. Quieter short field aircraft depended on exactly this trade. The study fed the broader quiet STOL research effort.
nasa-tm-19720016558-a-bibliographical-su:
William R Corliss prepared this bibliography on January 15, 1970, for NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It surveys writing on large scale systems and their control. Large scale systems range from power grids to whole cities. Controlling them was a young field with scattered literature. Corliss gathered that literature into one partly annotated list. The foreword frames the work as serving a better quality of life.

About four hundred references fill the survey. They are sorted into thirteen application areas. Large societal systems and large communication systems are among them. Short notes mark the value of key entries. A first author index closes the volume. The survey runs to about one hundred fifty pages.
parkman-la-salle:
La Salle and the Discovery of the Great West came out in 1869. Parkman made it Part Three of France and England in North America. The French explorer's descent of the Mississippi drives the whole book.

La Salle claims the river's mouth and the Gulf for France. Mutiny, hunger, and vast wild lands test him at every stage. His triumph ends in murder by his own weary men. Parkman tells the tale as high romance grounded in hard records. Many call it the most stirring story in early American history and exploration. La Salle's drive and doom grip readers to the end.
patriotic-plays-and-pageants-for-young-p: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Patriotic Plays and Pageants for Young People, the publisher's catalogue pages, title page, and copyright notice of 1912, with no play text visible. The catalogue describes Constance D'Arcy Mackay's one-act plays as dealing with the youth of American heroes, meant for schools, camps, and clubs. They can be used singly or linked into indoor or outdoor pageants, with directions for costumes, dances, and music.
peter-simple:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Peter Simple, dated 1834 in this record, is narrated by Peter himself. He calls himself the fool of the family, and by the old custom the greatest fool is sacrificed to the navy. At fourteen, having dreamed of a tailor's comfortable shopboard, he is chosen by general acclamation of his aunts and cousins.

His clergyman father sends him to London on the outside of the coach, booked in the way-bill like a parcel, carriage paid. Delivered to a stockbroker's house in St. Clement's Lane, Peter begins the midshipman's life that made the novel a classic of the sea.
podcast-dannyjones-ZRddaJfdalE:
Ed Barnhart and Luke Caverns join Danny Jones to talk about a lost Maya city in North America. The episode title calls it a super city found by an archaeologist. Barnhart is a scholar of Maya sites, and Caverns studies old sites in the field.

The guests describe the finds, the scale of the ruins, and why the site may change what we know of Maya reach. They also explain how new scans from the air helped spot the city under thick growth. Jones asks what the team plans to dig next. Listeners get a ground level view of a find that could redraw old maps.
podcast-joerogan-Uc5_z6buSLE:
Researcher Jimmy Corsetti shares new evidence for the Atlantis theory in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Corsetti, of the Bright Insight channel, argues that Plato's lost island matches a real site in the Sahara, the Richat Structure. His case has a large online following.

He walks Rogan through the rings of the Eye of the Sahara and how they echo Plato's account of rings of land and water. Rogan asks what would settle the claim and why experts resist it. The segment is a focused brief for one bold idea, delivered by its best-known advocate.
podcast-tuckercarlson-0aLXZj-oBLE:
Tucker Carlson addresses a packed Charlie Kirk event on the Epstein case. He jokes about the wild walkout music and the huge crowd. Then he turns to what others said that night.
