Carlson says he watched a rival host's take the day before. He offers a different view of the cover-up charge. The title calls the speech his message to America. He argues the case reveals how power guards itself. The tape preserves a live address to loyal fans who demanded answers their leaders would not give. He speaks as both friend and fellow fighter.
podcast-tuckercarlson-XrJUczTBILE:
Our airspace is being invaded, Carlson warns in a segment of Tucker Carlson's podcast, taking up the drone sightings that alarmed the country. Strange craft were reported over bases and coasts, and officials offered few clear answers. Carlson treats the silence as part of the story.

He reviews the sightings and the government's shifting statements, and asks why the world's best-funded military cannot say what flies over its own bases. The talk speaks to a wider public unease about control of the skies. The segment is a dated record of that scare, in the host's own alarmed and pointed style.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ykBp1WhdfLE:
Tucker Carlson speaks in a solo talk on what he calls Donald Trump's desecration of Easter. The title adds a warning to Christians in all lands. Carlson frames the charge as a man of faith, not just a host.

Carlson lays out the acts he says made the holy day a stage for pride and spite. He warns that faith bent to a man's brand will rot from within. He calls on Christians to hold their creed above any king or chief. Listeners get a stern sermon from a host to his own side. The library keeps the talk as a record of his stated view.
richard-hannay-02-greenmantle:
John Buchan's Greenmantle, dated 1916 in its heading, sends Richard Hannay back to secret war work. A dedication to Caroline Grosvenor says the tale was scribbled in odd places and moments over the past year. Buchan warns readers not to call its events improbable, for the war has driven that word out of use.

The dedication reports the cast: Sandy last heard of at Basra, Blenkiron cured and home in the States, and Peter in the Flying Corps. Chapter one finds Hannay convalescing at Furling in Hampshire after Loos. A telegram from Bullivant arrives as Sandy hunts the marmalade, and Hannay wonders why the Foreign Office wants an obscure major in double-quick time.
robinson-crusoe-in-words-of-one-syllable:
Mary Godolphin retold Defoe's Robinson Crusoe in words of one syllable, for the youngest readers. Her preface says the title explains the book, and her task was chiefly to reduce the common language to short words. Only the names Xury and Friday, and the titles of the pictures, break the rule.

One-syllable books of the day, she notes, offered little more than a few short, unlinked sentences in spelling books. She offers a whole famed story instead. It opens with Crusoe born at York, longing for the sea from childhood. He breaks loose from school and home, walks to Hull, and ships out, meeting a squall, a leak, and the pumps within days.
same-old-bill-eh-mable: Edward Streeter, of the 27th (N.Y.) Division, wrote Same Old Bill, Eh Mable, with twenty-seven black-and-white pictures by G. William Breck, also of the 27th Division, issued in New York in 1919. Streeter is named as author of Dere Mable and Thats Me All Over, Mable. The front pages also mark a cover page picture at the head of the list.
sergeant-york-and-his-people: A transcriber's note frames this book as a close, dramatic portrait of an ideal American soldier: thoughtful, brave, modest, kind, and loyal. The note pairs the book with a broad history of the World War, which it complements with a personal view. The pages at hand hold that note plus a glossary of hard words, with entries from light banter to land-bound terms. No chapter text or author's name appears in these opening pages, so the soldier's story itself cannot be told from what is shown here.
siege-of-washington-d-c-written-expressl:
Capt. F. Colburn Adams wrote this mock-heroic account of the siege of Washington for young readers, issued in New York in 1867. Adams had written The Story of a Trooper before this. A preface reports his publisher's fear that generals will take offense at the artist's liberties with their dignity.

Adams answers that great generals will laugh, while little ones were always fiercer against writers than against the enemy. He calls the siege the most remarkable military event in history, with tongue in cheek. Children of the Civil War era got war news as satire, aimed at pomp and panic in the capital.
sir-john-oldcastle:
The True and Honorable History of the Life of Sir John Oldcastle, the Good Lord Cobham, stands here as a play ascribed in part to William Shakespeare. A cast list crowds kings, lords, judges, bishops, rebels, and Lady Cobham around Henry the Fifth. The prologue speaks first to clear the hero's name.

No pampered glutton stands here, the prologue insists, answering those who knew Oldcastle as a stage fat knight. The true Cobham was a Lollard lord tried for heresy and hanged as a traitor. This old play gives the grave counter-tale: a faithful, wronged knight rather than a tavern joke.
stories-of-the-prophets-before-the-exile:
Isaac Landman wrote Stories of the Prophets (Before the Exile) for the Commission on Jewish Education of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations and the Central Conference of American Rabbis. Landman dedicated the book to his parents, who first brought him to the prophets.

The contents begin with The Shepherd of Tekoah, the prophet Amos, in chapters called An End to War, In the Days of Prosperity, and The Man Who Dared. The book retells the lives and messages of the early prophets as stories for young Jewish readers, stressing courage and justice. It was made as teaching material for religious schools, with a named board of rabbis and educators behind it.
style:
Walter Raleigh's Style, in its fifth impression from Edward Arnold at London in 1904, is a short essay on how English prose is written well. Raleigh had already written The English Novel and a critical essay on Robert Louis Stevenson, and he dedicates the little book, in Latin, to John Sampson, a librarian friend and fellow traveller.

A table of principal matters maps the argument, which treats the choice of words, the building of sentences, and the difference between writing that lives and writing that merely fills pages. Raleigh argues for clearness, force, and music in prose, and against fine writing that shows off. The essay became a standard pocket guide for students of English.
swingin-round-the-cirkle:
Petroleum V. Nasby, the pen name of David Ross Locke, published Swingin Round the Cirkle at Boston through Lee and Shepard in 1867, with illustrations by Thomas Nast. The book collects his letters to the public press during 1866, written as the semi-literate pastor of the Church of the New Dispensation and postmaster at Confederate Cross Roads, Kentucky.

Nasby's mock dedication addresses Androo Johnson, the pride and hope of Dimocrisy, who had swung around the entire circle of official honor from alderman to president. The letters, in thick dialect spelling, satirize President Johnson's famous Swing Around the Circle tour and the politics of Reconstruction, letting a foolish copperhead preacher damn his own cause with every sentence.
tarzan-the-terrible:
Edgar Rice Burroughs set Tarzan the Terrible in a hidden land of beast-men, with twenty-five chapters and a word list at the close. Chapter heads name strange peoples and beasts, from the Pithecanthropus and the Tor-o-don to the gryf and the city A-lur.

The opening stalks a great cat through a midnight jungle, silent on twigs and leaves, eyes round in the dark. That hunt sets the tone for a land where men with tails, temple rites, and blood-stained altars wait. Tarzan must cross pits, lion dens, and a forbidden garden to find what he seeks. Readers get one of the wildest of the Tarzan quests.
temple-trouble:
H. Beam Piper wrote Temple Trouble as a science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction, where it ran in April 1951. A head note sums the plot: time travelers plant fake wonders to win mining rights, but nature and men can plant counter-wonders too.

The tale opens through incense and altar smoke, where the idol Yat-Zar glares from a gold throne in a vast pillared temple. He bears three turquoise eyes, six arms, a gold-wire beard, and bird's feet, holding sword, torch, goblet, and scales. Readers get Piper's paratime world at work, where agents pose as gods and a staged faith starts to slip from their grip.
the-adventure-of-the-red-circle:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of the Red Circle as a Sherlock Holmes tale, told by Dr. Watson. It opens in the Baker Street rooms, where Holmes tries to brush off a landlady's plea and turn back to his scrapbook.

Mrs. Warren holds her ground with a landlady's grit and guile. She reminds Holmes that he once cleared up a case for her lodger Mr. Fairdale Hobbs, who never stopped praising his kindness. Soft words and a true debt of thanks move Holmes to sigh, lay down his gum brush, and hear her out. Readers get a case of a secret lodger, coded lamp signals, and an Italian vendetta worked out on London streets.
the-adventures-of-jimmie-dale: Frank L. Packard wrote The Adventures of Jimmie Dale, a crime tale. It splits into two parts. Part One is The Man in the Case. Part Two is The Woman in the Case. Chapters for the first part start with The Gray Seal. The Mother Lode and The Counterfeit Five follow. Devil's Work and The Man Higher Up come later. The second part brings The Crime Club. The Innocent Bystander and The Tocsin stand in that part.
the-adventures-of-peregrine-pickle:
Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle, a novel in which are included the Memoirs of a Lady of Quality. This first volume opens with an account of Mr. Gamaliel Pickle and the temper of his sister.

Gamaliel Pickle lives in a county of England bounded by the sea, a hundred miles from the capital. His father, a London merchant, rose from small starts to high honors in the city and a plump fortune. Yet he died, to his deep regret, just short of a plum — falling shy of his goal by less than fifteen thousand pounds. His dying charge bids his son copy his thrift till the gap is filled. Readers then follow young Peregrine through school, sea, and scams, in Smollett's broad, biting picaresque.
the-age-of-fable:
Thomas Bulfinch wrote The Age of Fable. It is the first part of Bulfinch's Mythology. This copy binds it in a complete one-volume set. The Age of Chivalry and Legends of Charlemagne stand with it. A note warns that the copy holds the Fable part alone. A publishers' preface fronts the work.

That preface ranks The Age of Fable with a famed set. Pilgrim's Progress, Gulliver's Travels, and The Arabian Nights are named. Robinson Crusoe is named as well. The book is called a work each reader must know. Some part of it is a must before an education can be called complete. It is also called a monument to Bulfinch's wide learning and care. Readers get Greek and Roman myths retold in clear prose. The book stayed the standard English guide to the old gods for more than a century.
the-auchensaugh-renovation-of-the-nation:
Renewed at Auchensaugh, near Douglas, on July 24, 1712, the National Covenant and Solemn League and Covenant are printed here with an acknowledgment of sins and a pledge to duties. A Philadelphia edition of 1880 sets that deed beside the Paisley edition of 1820 and the Belfast edition of 1835. It also prints a later renewal ordered at Philadelphia on October 8, 1880, by the Reformed Presbytery.

A long preface defends the 1712 act as the one faithful renewal of the covenants. Its writers argue that opponents first attacked this deed, removed it from terms of communion, and in Scotland struck it out in 1822. Readers get both the old church pledges and a sharp case for keeping them unchanged.
the-autocrat-of-the-breakfast-table: Oliver Wendell Holmes's famous series of witty breakfast-table monologues, first published in The Atlantic Monthly in 1857. The Autocrat holds forth on everything from poetry and science to human nature, in essays that blend humor, philosophy, and good talk. They made Holmes America's most beloved man of letters and invented a whole style of familiar essay.
the-babylonian-story-of-the-deluge-as-to:
E. A. Wallis Budge retells the Babylonian flood story from Assyrian tablets found at Nineveh. He begins with Layard's digs in 1845 to 1847 and again in 1849 to 1851. The ruins lie across the Tigris from Mosul, on a site long linked by local and religious tradition to the ancient city.

Budge describes mounds, walls, and palaces built by kings such as Sargon II, Sennacherib, and Esarhaddon. One mound holds the palace and library of Ashur-bani-pal. Setting the scene in this detail lets readers see where the tablets lay before he turns to what the flood text itself says.
the-beast-in-the-jungle:
Henry James's tale, in a Martin Secker edition of 1915, opens at Weatherend, a great house shown to luncheon guests. John Marcher wanders through rooms full of pictures, heirlooms, and treasures, feeling pressed by their poetry and history. Among the visitors he meets May Bartram again.

Her face troubles him pleasantly, like the sequel to something whose start he has lost. She, by contrast, seems not to have lost the thread of their earlier meeting. That uneven memory drives the opening chapter. Marcher senses a shared past and a secret between them, while James lingers over glances, rooms, and half-formed feeling.
the-beetle:
Richard Marsh wrote this horror tale of an Egyptian beetle curse in 1897. It came out the same year as Dracula, and in its first year it sold more than Stoker's book. Marsh was a brisk hand at tales of dread for the broad public of his day.

A shape shifting being, part man, part woman, part beast, comes to London from Egypt. It seeks revenge on a young man of Parliament for a wrong done in a past age. The book caught the pulp dread of the 1890s in its most pure and wild form.
the-book-of-art-for-young-people: Agnes Ethel Conway and Sir Martin Conway wrote The Book of Art for Young People, put out in London by A. and C. Black. The book has sixteen full-page plates in color. It first came out in September 1909 as The Children's Book of Art, and was put out again in 1914, 1927, and 1935. The front plate is Red Riding Hood, from a work by G. F. Watts in the Birmingham Art Gallery. A note thanks lords, a herald, and friends for leave to use works and verse.
the-boy-ranchers-on-the-trail-or-the-dia: Willard F. Baker wrote The Boy Ranchers on the Trail, or The Diamond X After Cattle Rustlers. The chapter list starts with The Round-Up and A Curious Instrument. Startling News, The Scratched Safe, and The Broken Bottle come next. Then come Missing Steers, Four Eyes, and Throwing the Rope. A fire, hard questions, and a watch tower crowd the mid heads. The Signal and Four Eyes-No Eyes lead to A Big Raid, On the Trail, and Wild Country. The Boiling Spring is the last head shown.
the-bravo-a-tale:
J. Fenimore Cooper opens The Bravo: A Tale, in a form dated 1872, with a preface on how ill the world sorts its state terms. States are called monarchies or republics, he says, but each name hides wild splits.

Cooper says his aim was to give his own folk a picture of the social system of one of the so-called republics of the old world. He made no try at true men of the past in their grave dress. He set out the day-to-day work of Venetian state craft, and points to the known work of M. Daru for proof of the likeness. The preface then weighs how freedom grew in Europe, right by right won from rulers. That, he says, splits from the American rule, where the folk grant rights to the state.
the-bronze-eagle: Baroness Orczy wrote The Bronze Eagle: A Story of the Hundred Days, put out in New York by the George H. Doran Company with rights dated 1915. Orczy had also written The Laughing Cavalier and The Scarlet Pimpernel. A list of her books stands in front, naming A Bride of the Plains, El Dorado, Meadowsweet, The Noble Rogue, and Petticoat Rule. The subtitle alone sets the scene: the Hundred Days, Napoleon's last return to power. Only the front pages are shown, with no page of the tale itself.
the-campaign-of-chancellorsville: The Campaign of Chancellorsville, by Theodore A. Dodge, is dedicated to the Military Historical Society of Massachusetts, and its opening pages give the table of contents alone. Twenty-eight chapters and more are headed. They move from Hooker's appointment and the Army of Northern Virginia to the cavalry raid against Lee's communications. Jackson's march and attack, the Eleventh Corps, Fairview, and Sedgwick's operations follow. No narrative page is shown.
the-campaigns-of-the-british-army-at-was:
The Campaigns of the British Army at Washington and New Orleans, by G. R. Gleig, chaplain-general to the forces, appears here in a new edition dated 1879. Its advertisement insists the work is the only connected and authentic account of those expeditions. It is not a loose relation of hearsay. It was compiled from a journal kept during the progress of the events it describes.

The campaigns belong to the close of the late American war. The contents begin with the embarkation of the troops and their passage. Then comes the march to Bordeaux, before the history turns toward America. The claim the edition stakes is documentary: a connected history of two famous expeditions, written from notes made on the spot while the events were still unfolding.
the-choir-invisible: James Lane Allen wrote this novel, issued as a Project Gutenberg text in September 2000. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and release dates, plus a line crediting Susan L. Farley as transcriber.The book itself never opens here. The header is dated September 2000 and numbered 2316 in the Gutenberg series.
the-clue-of-the-twisted-candle:
Edgar Wallace opens this thriller with a delayed train and a wet walk. The 4.15 from Victoria to Lewes has been held at Three Bridges by a derailment. John Lexman catches a late connection to Beston Tracey, but the wagonette that links the village with the outside world has already gone.

The station-master offers to telephone the village and have Briggs come down in half an hour. Lexman looks at the dripping landscape, shrugs, and says he will walk. He leaves his bag at the station, buttons his mackintosh to his chin, and sets out into the rain for Little Tracey, two miles off. The downpour looks set to last all night, and the high hedges run like leafy cascades. He stops under a big tree to light his pipe, bowl turned down, and walks on. Wallace sets his man alone in foul weather before the candle clue appears.
the-court-of-boyville: William Allen White, author of The Real Issue, wrote The Court of Boyville, dated 1898, with pictures by Orson Lowell and, for the first story, Gustav Verbeek. Its contents list a prologue and tales such as The Martyrdom of Mealy Jones, A Recent Confederate Victory, James Sears: A Naughty Person, and The Herb Called Hearts-Ease. A short verse asks where Boyville lies and how a traveler might find the road back to its shady rows of corn. Only the front matter and contents are present here.
the-cruise-of-the-cachalot-round-the-wor:
Frank T. Bullen, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society who sailed as first mate, wrote The Cruise of the Cachalot about a round-the-world hunt for sperm whales. He dedicates the book to Miss Emily Hensley, in thanks for thirty years of friendship and practical help, calling himself her humble pupil.

In his preface Bullen claims a first: a cruise of a South Sea whaler told from the seaman's standpoint. Two older books on the subject, by ships' surgeons F. Debell Bennett and Thomas Beale, were written for science and have long been out of print, though Beale's stays the standard work on the sperm whale. Bullen aims at the general reader instead, setting out the methods and dangers of a calling the public knows nothing about, from his own observation and never at second hand.
the-devil-s-disciple:
George Bernard Shaw's The Devil's Disciple is a play in three acts. Act I opens in 1777 at the bleakest hour before a wintry dawn. Mrs. Dudgeon of New Hampshire sits up in the kitchen and general dwelling room of her farmhouse on the outskirts of Websterbridge.

The stage directions paint her as no prepossessing woman. Her face is cut deep by the barren forms of a dead Puritanism, which have soured her temper and hardened her pride. She has worked hard and gained only dominion and detestation in her sordid home. She also has an unquestioned name for piety and respectability among neighbors, to whom drink still tempts more than religion. They conceive goodness simply as self-denial.
the-discovery-of-the-source-of-the-nile:
John Hanning Speke wrote The Discovery of the Source of the Nile. A page of facts at the front records that Speke, born in 1827, served in the Punjab, left in 1854 to explore Somaliland. He found Lake Tanganyika with Burton and Lake Victoria on his own, and, with Grant, was the first European to cross equatorial Africa; he died in 1864.

An editor's note adds that Speke was thirty-six when his Nile journal appeared. He had entered the army in 1844 and served ten years in India, through the Punjab campaign, already dreaming of African exploration. He joined the expedition then preparing under Lieutenant Burton for the Somali country, was wounded by the Somalis. He came home on sick leave as the Crimean War broke out, serving through it before joining another expedition in December 1856.
the-elder-brother-the-works-of-francis-b: The Elder Brother heads a volume of plays by Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher. Their life years head the page: 1584 to 1616, and 1579 to 1625. Arnold Glover and A. R. Waller edited the text for Cambridge University Press in 1906. The volume also holds The Spanish Curate, Wit Without Money, and Beggars Bush. Only the title matter and contents are present here. No scene from any play follows.
the-enchanted-castle:
Margaret Ostler receives the dedication of The Enchanted Castle, dated September 1907 from Soho. In verse, E Nesbit thanks Peggy for bringing the airs of heath and moor through her door. Chapter one names the three children. Gerald is called Jerry. James is called Jimmy. Kathleen is Cathy, or Puss Cat, to her brothers.

The three board at schools in a small western town, boys apart from girls. Holidays lead them to a great house with a magic ring and stone beasts that stir. Nesbit blends plain child talk with true wonder.
the-evil-eye-or-the-black-spector-the-wo:
William Carleton's The Evil Eye; or, The Black Spector opens with a short preface on its theme. The belief in the evil eye, Carleton says, has spread to every land on earth, and in his own youth it stood as settled dogma. Yet schooling and knowledge are wearing it thin, he notes, and soon such idle faiths will fade.

Some lore he traces to the Druids, whom he respects save for tales of human sacrifice. His tale then shows the blight at work in Irish farm life: envy, curses, and fear. Carleton writes from inside the world he shows.
the-fool-errant-being-the-memoirs-of-fra:
Maurice Hewlett framed The Fool Errant as the memoirs of Francis-Antony Strelley, a citizen of Lucca, and gives himself the role of editor. The book came out in July 1905, given to J. M. Barrie.

Strelley tells his own tale in the first person: a plea for his acts, a love for Aurelia, a fall, and a road taken as a pilgrim. He meets a pedlar of crosses, falls in with Fra Palamone, is held in bondage, and quarrels and makes up with Virginia. Hewlett builds a bright, old-world tale of love, pride, and a fool's slow schooling in Italy.
the-framework-of-home-rule:
Erskine Childers wrote The Framework of Home Rule in 1911 to set out how Ireland might rule itself. Childers was known for The Riddle of the Sands and for works on cavalry and war.

His chapters trace Ireland and America side by side: settlement, revolt, Grattan's Parliament, and the Union. He then sets Canada, Australia, and South Africa next to Ireland, drawing the points of likeness before he states Ireland's case as it stood in his day. The last chapter builds the frame itself: the parts of the problem and the shape of a home rule law that could hold both Irish claims and the tie to Britain.
the-further-adventures-of-jimmie-dale: Frank L. Packard wrote The Further Adventures of Jimmie Dale as tales of a rich man who robs as the Gray Seal, printed in 1919. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name Smarlinghue, a man with a scar, a diamond pendant, cries of death to the Gray Seal, a bond robbery, voices of the underworld, a sanctuary, and a secret room. No chapter text shows up in these pages, so the capers cannot be told from these opening pages alone.
the-great-doctrines-of-the-bible: Rev. William Evans wrote The Great Doctrines of the Bible. The book grew out of classroom lectures, set in lasting form at his students' request. Only the front matter and foreword are present here. The contents list doctrines of God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit, then of man, the church, the Scriptures, angels, and Satan. Salvation covers repentance, faith, regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, and prayer. The last things cover the Second Coming, the Judgment, and the reward of the righteous. His method, he says, is Biblical, not dogmatic.
the-greylock-a-fairy-tale:
Georg Ebers wrote The Greylock, a fairy tale. Long ago stood a land fairer than any other. Beside a lake of deepest blue lay the castle of the Duke who ruled it. In days past, the Knight Wendelin rode there with his squire George. They came on a scene of ruin: fields gone to waste, columns split, statues with broken noses. Vines had once climbed terraces held by the old walls. Now foxes and bats lived among them.

The knight wondered what had befallen the place. He took his horse down to drink. The water tasted sweet, nothing like the salt Dead Sea. Then a sound reached him from a grotto, sad and sweet, like an unhappy woman's voice. Wendelin had ridden out in search of adventures. Seven dragons' tail-tips hung from George's saddle. A woman in peril was the chance a knight could wish for.
the-house-of-mystery-an-episode-in-the-c: Will Irwin wrote this 1910 novel as an episode in the career of Rosalie Le Grange, a clairvoyant, with illustrations by Frederick C. Yohn. Only the front matter, contents, and list of illustrations are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. The chapter titles trace a case taking shape: an unknown girl, a Mr. Norcross, a mysterious light that wavers, Rosalie's first and second reports, a girl named Annette who lies and then tells the truth, and a chapter drawn mainly from the newspapers.
the-house-on-the-beach-a-realistic-tale:
George Meredith opens this tale with a general reflection. Great officials retire and review their careers. They learn that small eccentricities damage them most. Grand failures matter less than trifles. He compares such slips to the heel of Achilles. A mother's hand held her child at that spot. Common people's oddities entertain the crowd. Dignity makes the same behavior dangerous for the great.

His example is Mr. Tinman. Tinman cannot resist a bargain at a herring auction. He climbed from a tiny shop to a large business. His marketing mother supplied his virtues. He then retired as a gentleman to Crikswich. There he rents the cheapest house he can find. It is the house on the beach. He lives imposingly on five percent. His shop once yielded fifty.
the-jungle: Sinclair's 1906 Jungle exposed Chicago meatpacking horrors through Jurgis. It sickened a nation. The Tower library holds the full text. It ground workers. Rats ran. Laws passed. Outrage boiled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-lani-people:
J. F. Bone writes science fiction about Jac Kennon, a new veterinary graduate with little money and a spaceman ticket. Kennon spots a boxed ad in a medical journal from the planet Kardon. The post offers a five year livestock contract, furnished quarters, a fine hospital, and fifteen thousand credits a year.

Pay that high for a beginner makes him suspect a catch. He checks Kardon currency and finds it sound, then counts what the contract could save toward his own clinic. Bone sets up a frontier job story where a dream offer may hide a hard truth about the Lani.
the-little-red-hen-an-old-english-folk-t: The Little Red Hen, described as an old English folk tale, was retold and illustrated by Florence White Williams and published by the Saalfield Publishing Company, with a 1918 copyright. Only the title pages and the first lines of the tale are present here, so the story itself does not appear beyond its opening. Those lines place a little red hen in a barnyard, walking about in her picketty-pecketty fashion and scratching everywhere for worms.
the-makers-and-teachers-of-judaism-from-: Charles Foster Kent, Professor of Biblical Literature at Yale, wrote The Makers and Teachers of Judaism. It covers the period from Jerusalem's fall to the death of Herod the Great, dated 1911, with maps. Only the title page and contents are present, so the sections do not appear. The contents treat the exile and revival of the community. They cover the Jews in Palestine and Egypt, and the colony and temple of Jahu at Elephantine. Ezekiel's message to his scattered countrymen and the closing years of Babylonian rule follow.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: The complete Memoirs of Jacques Casanova de Seingalt, covering 1725 to 1798, appear in the rare unabridged London edition of 1894. Arthur Machen made the English version, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons added. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the memoir text itself does not appear. The contents promise an account of Casanova at Dux, prefaces by translator and author, and a first volume of Venetian years. Its opening episodes treat his childhood and his time as a cleric in Naples.
the-mind-of-the-child-part-ii-the-develo: Only the publisher's series pages are present for The Mind of the Child, Part II, so the book's own title page, author, and text do not appear. The pages describe the International Education Series, edited by William T. Harris, the United States Commissioner of Education. The series aimed to gather the best writings on education into a uniform course of reading for teachers. Volumes listed include Rosenkranz on the philosophy of education, Painter's history of education, Laurie's survey of universities, and Froebel's Education of Man.
the-nameless-castle:
Maurus Jokai's The Nameless Castle, translated from the Hungarian by S. E. Boggs under the author's supervision, was published in New York by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1898. A portrait of Jokai fronts the volume, which belongs to a Hungarian edition of his works. Before the novel, Jokai addresses the English translation of his works directly.

Earlier English versions, he complains, were often made from other languages rather than the Hungarian text, or reached the public marred by faults for want of a final reading. This edition uses an authorised text, and Doubleday and McClure hold sole rights for future English translations. Jokai then finds many common traits between the United States and Hungary: constitutional freedom, respect for women and labour, and rapid growth of towns.
the-napoleon-of-the-people:
Honore de Balzac's The Napoleon of the People, translated by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell, is framed by a preparer's note. The tale first appeared in The Country Doctor, where Goguelat, an old soldier who served in one of Napoleon's infantry regiments, tells it to a group of peasants. It later joined a Russian-derived collection of folk-tales of Napoleon.

Goguelat begins at the beginning: Napoleon was born in Corsica, a French island under an Italian sun where families kill each other for generations over nothing. His mother, the handsomest and shrewdest of women, dedicated him to God to escape the dangers of infancy, having dreamed the world was on fire the day he was born. At Eylau, Goguelat swears, bullets that carried off soldiers like flies respected the Emperor's head.
the-native-born-or-the-rajah-s-people:
I. A. R. Wylie's novel The Native Born, or The Rajah's People, dated 1910 and illustrated by John Newton Howitt, opens with a preface dated May 9, 1910. Wylie confesses that a preface to a novel once seemed out of place to her, since an author supposedly owed everything to imagination alone. Experience taught her otherwise, and she thanks Mr. Hughes Massie for his enthusiastic help in launching her first serious literary effort.

A contents list for Book I follows. A prologue chapter gives way to The Dancing Is Resumed, Nehal Singh, and Circe. Archibald Travers Plays Bridge closes the visible list at Chapter V, mixing Indian names with English social scenes in a way that suits the double title.
the-nicomachean-ethics-of-aristotle:
Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics is presented here with an introduction by J. A. Smith. A contents list shows the introduction, the ten books of the Ethics, and notes; no translator is named in the pages shown. Smith begins from a structural claim: the Ethics forms one half of a single treatise whose other half is the Politics, and both treat the same subject.

That subject, Smith explains, is what Aristotle calls the philosophy of human affairs, or political and social science. Together the two works hold his whole theory of human conduct, meaning every activity not aimed merely at knowledge. The Ethics closes by pointing forward to the Politics and sketching its order of enquiry, an order the finished Politics does not actually follow, as Smith notes.
the-pearl-story-book-a-collection-of-tal: Mrs. Colman wrote The Pearl Story Book, a collection of tales original and selected, published in 1850 as the third item in her New Juvenile Series. Present here are a series list, a title page, and the start of a contents list; the tales themselves are not. The list opens with The Turtle-Doves of Carmel, about a young English musician wintering at Mount Carmel and a kind old monk. Titles for The Dying Child, Frightened by a Cow, and The Red Shoes follow.
the-philosophy-of-style:
Herbert Spencer wrote The Philosophy of Style. Part I treats causes of force in language that depend on economy of the mental energies. Spencer opens with Tristram Shandy's wonder at a man who reasoned well without knowing the names of his tools. Good writing, like good reasoning, owes more to practice and natural aptitude than to rules, he grants.

A clear head, a quick imagination, and a sensitive ear make most rhetorical precepts needless. Still, knowing the principles can help, above all in revision. Spencer complains that maxims on style stand as isolated dogmas, not deduced from one first principle. His essay seeks that principle in saving the reader's mental energy.
the-phoenix-and-the-turtle:
William Shakespeare's poem The Phoenix and the Turtle is a funeral song for two birds. It opens by calling the bird of loudest lay, on the sole Arabian tree, to be herald and trumpet. The shrieking owl, harbinger of the fiend, is barred from the session. Every fowl of tyrant wing is excluded, save the eagle, feathered king.

The swan, priest in surplice white, must sing the requiem, and the crow joins the mourners. Then the anthem begins: love and constancy is dead, phoenix and turtle fled in a mutual flame. The poem praises a love in which two distinct hearts held one essence, with division none. It is among Shakespeare's most riddling works.
the-pilgrim-s-progress-in-words-of-one-s:
Mary Godolphin's The Pilgrim's Progress in Words of One Syllable retells Bunyan's allegory using one-syllable words throughout. Names of persons and places keep their original form, as the single exception. Her preface explains the aim plainly. The volume serves adult beginners who learn to read late in life, just as much as it serves children. Earlier books on the same plan had been used as school prizes.

Short words, Godolphin argues, spare new readers the labour of dividing and sounding out long ones. The story then starts in the familiar way, retold in brief plain lines. A man in rags stands turned from his own house. He holds a book, and a great load lies on his back. Reading, he weeps, shakes with fear, and cries out for his soul before going home to his wife and children.
the-poet-at-the-breakfast-table:
Oliver Wendell Holmes's The Poet at the Breakfast Table is the third series of his Breakfast-Table conversations. His preface explains that a slight dramatic background sets off a few talkers and writers, helped by silent supernumeraries. Some characters will seem like old acquaintances to readers of the earlier papers. One figure stands for a class Holmes says had greatly multiplied: the scientific specialist.

His example is an entomologist who confines himself rigidly to beetles. The division of labour, Holmes jokes, has reached every profession. It reaches even surgeons who will treat a dislocation of one shoulder but not the other. Against the specialists he sets wide-ranging minds such as Cuvier, Buckle, and Herbert Spencer. He also introduces the humorist behind a work on the universe. A young astronomer's verse speaks for the natural man, and a lady's letter gives fair play to gentle, reverential conservatism.
the-poetics-of-aristotle: Aristotle's Poetics is presented here in S. H. Butcher's translation. Here only the title page, a transcriber's note, and an analysis of contents appear, so the treatise itself is absent. The note explains that Greek words kept by the translator are spelled out letter by letter inside braces. Readers without Greek may skip them. The analysis lists twenty-three heads. They run from imitation as the common principle of poetry to the definition of tragedy, unity of plot, reversal and recognition, diction, and epic poetry.
the-point-of-honor-a-military-tale:
Joseph Conrad's The Point of Honor, a military tale, was published by the McClure Company at New York in 1908, with illustrations by Dan Sayre Groesbeck. Conrad opens with Napoleon the First. His career, Conrad writes, resembled a single duel fought against all Europe.

Napoleon, Conrad notes, disliked duelling between officers of his army. He held little respect for its traditions. Yet one story of duelling became a legend of the imperial wars. Two cavalry officers pursued a private contest through years of universal carnage, like artists gilding refined gold. Illustration captions name one of them, Colonel D'Hubert. They promise a fight no more at the frontispiece, a sylph-like form on a couch, and an angry clash of arms in a prim garden.
the-professor-at-the-breakfast-table: Oliver Wendell Holmes prefaces a revised edition of The Professor at the Breakfast-Table by warning that nearly a quarter century has passed. Statements true then need not hold now; the trotting-horse record, for one, has fallen. These papers followed the Autocrat and faced the trial of all second comers, as Paradise Regained and the second Faust warn. Some readers preferred the sequel, others attacked opinions now harmless as a nihilist's utterances. The pages at hand hold this preface only, not the breakfast-table papers.
the-queen-of-the-pirate-isle:
Bret Harte introduces nine-year-old Polly, a plump and good-humored girl who has never been to sea and lives nowhere near an island, yet rules as queen of a pirate isle in play. The narrator lists her earlier invented roles, from beggar child and schoolmistress to preacher and Indian maiden.

Polly's characters last for days or weeks and are usually ended by a convenient death, though some return with explanations. A nursery voyage in a Chinese junk, with cousin Hickory Hunt and page Wan Lee, launches the pirate game after a sudden local hurricane. The tale charms as a study of children's imagination at full stretch.
the-quilt-that-jack-built-how-he-won-the: Annie Fellows Johnston's name heads a publisher's catalogue of the Little Colonel books, listing story volumes, house party and holiday titles, Arizona and boarding-school adventures, and boxed sets with prices. Holiday and Cosy Corner editions are priced separately, and Mary Ware titles extend the series beyond its first heroine. Only the publisher's catalogue pages are present here, so Jack's quilt story itself does not appear.
the-red-rover-a-tale: James Fenimore Cooper's sea tale appears in a one-volume edition. The edition is dated 1855. It holds a preface and thirty-two chapters. The chapters are listed without titles. Only the title page and motto are present here. The opening of the contents list appears with them. A preface heading stands at the end. The rover's story itself does not appear on these pages.
the-religious-spirit-of-the-slavs-three-:
Father Nicolai Velimirovic was a Serbian priest. He taught theology at the University of Belgrade. He gave three Lent lectures in 1916. The lectures treat Slav Orthodoxy first. They treat Slav revolutionary Catholicism next. They end with the Slav religious spirit itself. A wartime sermon series at St. Margaret's, Westminster, printed them. Lecture one begins with a famous case. It opens with Tolstoy's excommunication by the Holy Synod.

Velimirovic says the world split in sympathy over that case. The West favored Tolstoy, and the Orthodox East favored the Synod. Russia still rejected Tolstoy with compassion. Europe approved him with less mercy, he argues. A parable of grass voices his deeper fear. The grass wants to return to seed. Civilizational retreat is the danger he names. The lectures offer an insider's wartime theology.
the-right-and-wrong-uses-of-the-bible: R. Heber Newton sets out seven lectures under a homily motto saying God's true word is contained in Scripture. Contents divide an unreal Bible from a real one, then take up wrong uses twice before turning to right critical, historical, ethical, and spiritual uses. Here only the title pages, publisher's list of Newton's other books, and contents together with two long motto quotations are present, so the lectures themselves do not appear.
the-shuttle: Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Shuttle is represented here by its title page and contents alone. Forty-one chapters are listed, with no chapter text following. The weaving of the shuttle opens the book. Young Lady Anstruthers and a lack of perception follow. Later headings place the action on both sides of the Atlantic. A second-class passenger, Lady Jane Grey, and Ughtred appear. G. Selden is introduced and his thread followed later. The tidal wave and closed corridors come near the end.
the-silent-isle:
Arthur Christopher Benson, Fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, published The Silent Isle in 1913. He dedicated it to Percy Lubbock under a Latin epigraph. The first essay gives the place its name. Yet in no land has he lived with so little sight and sound of water, he admits. Water oozes from field to drain and trickles to the great seaward sluice, he writes.

The whole place still feels like an island, remote and unapproachable, Benson says. A great black plain of quivering soil runs up to long, low, green hills. The village a mile away looks like a straggling seaport town. The encircling fen is trackless like water, he adds. No short cuts or footpaths cross it. Vast sky gives largeness to the scene, with rolling cloud-banks overhead.
the-story-of-doctor-dolittle: Hugh Lofting tells and illustrates the history of Doctor Dolittle's peculiar life at home and astonishing adventures in foreign parts, published by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York in 1920. Only the title pages are present here, with printing facts. A printing history runs from August 1920 to an eleventh printing in April 1923. A note says Hugh Walpole introduced the tenth printing. Lofting's dedication follows. He dedicates the book to all children, in years and in heart. The doctor's adventures themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-my-life-with-her-letters-18:
Helen Keller's autobiography appears in a special edition. It holds extra chapters by Keller. Her letters from 1887 to 1901 appear too. John Albert Macy adds an account of her education. He drew it from her teacher Anne Mansfield Sullivan's reports and letters. Keller dedicates the book to Alexander Graham Bell, who taught the deaf to speak, and the editor's preface explains the plan in three parts.

Keller's own story and her letters give a full account of her life. They give it as far as she can give one, the editor says. She cannot explain much of her education herself. Sullivan's reports and letters therefore supplement the autobiography, with thanks to the Ladies' Home Journal for its photographs and to friends who lent letters and anecdotes.
the-story-of-the-champions-of-the-round-:
Howard Pyle wrote and illustrated this Arthurian volume. It is the second of four such books. He undertook them in 1902. They retell the legend of King Arthur and his knights. A reissue introduction explains the book's matter. It first appeared in 1905. It recounts the saga of three famous knights. Percival, Tristram, and Launcelot of the Lake are the three. The reissue keeps the original format. Pyle's illustrations and decorations appear in it.

The introduction quotes critic Elizabeth Nesbitt calling Pyle's period a golden age in children's literature, in which his twofold genius as creative artist and born storyteller continually enriched itself. A contents list then opens the story of Launcelot, telling how he came forth from the enchanted castle of the Lake and was made a knight by Arthur.
the-submarine-boys-for-the-flag-deeding-: Victor G. Durham's sixth book of the Submarine Boys series, dated 1910, deeds the boys' lives to Uncle Sam. Only the title page appears here, with two other pieces. A contents list of twenty-four chapters stands first. The opening lines of chapter one follow. Jabez Holt calls out from a hotel window at Dunhaven. He asks whether a stranger speaks German. The titles promise chart-marking spies. A lesson in security and information follows. Daisy Huston decides for the flag. The adventure itself does not appear beyond its threshold.
the-survey-of-cornwall-and-an-epistle-co: Richard Carew of Antonie wrote this survey of Cornwall. An epistle on the excellencies of the English tongue goes with it. A life of the author appears too. The new edition was printed in London and Penzance in 1769. Only the title page and the opening of a list of subscribers are present in this record, headed by Sir John St. Aubyn of Clowance, taking twenty copies, and running through Helston, St. Just, and St. Ives names to Penzance merchants and attorneys, so Carew's survey itself does not appear.
the-swiss-family-robinson-told-in-words-:
Mary Godolphin retells the Swiss Family Robinson for the youngest readers. She uses words of one syllable. Chapter one wastes no time. The narrator will say nothing of the voyage at first. The ship has spent six days in a storm. She is driven far out of her course. Her masts lie in splints on deck. A leak gains on the pumps.

The father gathers his four sons. God can save them if it pleases Him, he tells them. If this is their last hour, they will at least go down side by side. His wife kneels calmly to pray. Then comes the cry of land and a shock. The ship has struck a rock. The crew have launched the boats and left the family behind. The hull is wedged fast on the rocks, though. A trace of land to the south restores hope.
the-tale-of-mrs-tiggy-winkle:
Frederick Warne published Beatrix Potter's Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle in 1905, offered to the real little Lucie of Newlands. Lucie lives at a farm called Little-town and keeps losing her pocket-handkerchiefs. One day she comes into the farmyard crying over three lost handkerchiefs and a pinafore. She asks Tabby Kitten whether they have been seen.

The kitten only goes on washing her white paws, so Lucie asks a speckled hen, who runs clucking into a barn. Cock Robin on a twig looks at her sideways and flies over a stile. Each animal she questions sends her further along her search. Potter builds a small mystery out of a child's everyday loss.
the-trail-of-the-white-mule:
B. M. Bower sends Casey Ryan into chapter one of The Trail of the White Mule behind the wheel of a dark blue touring car with a kinked fender and a broken headlight. Casey slides out of halted traffic, shies from a clanging street car, and misses a red truck by two inches before the traffic officer overtakes him. The Irish officer, bigger and madder than Casey, offers him a pale, expensive ticket, which Casey crumples unread into his pocket.

Casey offers to lick the tar out of him and proposes calling the undertaker first. The officer, softened by the Little Woman beside Casey, advises forfeiting bail instead of taking thirty days, since this is far from Casey's first offence. Bower's comic Westerner, a desert driver lost among city rules, starts his story already in trouble with the law.
the-travels-of-sir-john-mandeville:
Macmillan's 1900 edition of The Travels of Sir John Mandeville, presenting the Cotton manuscript version in modern spelling, opens with a bibliographical note on the book's strange history. The Travels were first edited anonymously in 1725 from the Cotton text, the only authority for that version. Printed editions from Wynkyn de Worde in 1499 onward had followed an inferior translation, complete with an unperceived gap in the middle, which had already won the upper hand before printing began.

A third version, from the Egerton manuscript, was printed by G. F. Warner for the Roxburghe Club in 1889 with the French text and praised notes. The note explains why this edition matters to scholars. Mandeville's fabulous fourteenth-century journey to the Holy Land and beyond follows, in the version modern editors trust most.
the-voice-of-the-people:
Ellen Glasgow's The Voice of the People was copyrighted in 1900 and issued by Doubleday, Page in New York. Book one is called Fair Weather at Kingsborough. The opening scene falls on the last day of circuit court in the old court-house there, as jury, clerk, and judge disperse into a straggling crowd of spectators.

Glasgow lingers on the room's smells of bad tobacco and farm-stained clothing, and on a breeze scattering them as the doorway crowd parts. The judge picks his way toward sunken stone steps outside. A dedication to Rebe Gordon Glasgow precedes the novel, and an author's list names her earlier books The Descendant and Phases of an Inferior Planet.
the-voyage-of-the-beagle:
Charles Darwin explains in his preface how he came to sail on the Beagle. Captain Fitz Roy wanted a scientific companion aboard and offered part of his own accommodations. Darwin volunteered, the Admiralty sanctioned the plan, and five years of friendship and steady help from Fitz Roy and the officers followed.

The volume presents the voyage as a journal, mixing its history with sketches of natural history and geology for general readers. Darwin says this edition condenses and corrects earlier parts for popular reading. Specialists are pointed to the larger Zoology volumes by Owen, Waterhouse, Gould, Jenyns, and Bell, helped by a thousand-pound Treasury grant toward publication costs. Habits and ranges accompany his own species descriptions.
the-voyages-of-doctor-dolittle: Hugh Lofting illustrated his own Voyages of Doctor Dolittle, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York in 1922. The pages present here show a picture-history plate and the title page, so the story itself does not appear. The plate, labelled the Popsipetel picture-history of King Jong Thinkalot, lists six scenes: the doctor's landing on the island, his meeting with the beetle, and his freeing of the lost families. Further scenes show him making fire, leading the people to victory in war, and being crowned king.
the-water-witch-or-the-skimmer-of-the-se:
James Fenimore Cooper's Water-Witch, or The Skimmer of the Seas, appears here complete in one volume, dated 1871. A French motto from Molière asks what the devil someone was doing in that galley. Chapter one opens not with smugglers but with geography, praising the fine estuary where Hudson, Hackensack, Passaic, and Raritan waters meet the ocean.

Cooper credits New York's extraordinary prosperity to that fortunate land-and-water arrangement, sheltered by Nassau and Staten islands. Manhattan sits at the precise desirable point, he argues, where millions might live while ships load near every door. The ground even supplies building material. His tale of a mysterious skimmer begins inside a hymn to the harbour that shelters her.
the-way-of-an-eagle: Ethel M. Dell, author of The Rocks of Valpré, published The Way of an Eagle with Cassell in London in 1919. A frontispiece caption pictures Muriel seated on the ground with her face buried in her hands, with the lines numbered sixteen and seventeen. The pages present here give the title and a partial contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. Opening chapters take the eagle's flight, then banish a girl to a mountain and promise a widow's mite. Later headings trace friends, a waiting, and storm.
the-white-people:
Arthur Machen, a Welsh writer of tales of dread, wrote this strange work in 1904. It here stands in its Wikisource form, from an old print. Machen held that the old pagan world did not die, but hid in the hills and in the blood.

A frame talk on the nature of evil opens the book, in a calm and grave style. Then comes the Green Book, the diary of a girl who roams the Welsh hills to dark rites. The tale is held by many to be one of the high marks of horror in English.
the-winter-s-tale: Only editorial notes from Project Gutenberg appear at the front of the record, signed by its founder, Michael S. Hart. The notes warn readers that old spelling oddities were left unchanged on purpose. Early printers sometimes swapped letters when their type ran short. A few lines from Hamlet show the effect. The play itself does not begin within the pages shown here.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-08-talm: Volume eight of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser in 1908, shows its contents and nothing more here. Talmage opens with a sermon called A Bloody Monster. Spurgeon's Songs in the Night follows. Phillips Brooks appears with The Pride of Life. D. L. Moody asks, What Think Ye of Christ? The sermons themselves are absent from the pages included here.
theresa-marchmont-or-the-maid-of-honour-:
Mrs. Charles Gore published Theresa Marchmont, or, The Maid of Honour in London in 1824. A French epigraph from La Bruyere compares the court to a marble building, hard but polished. Chapter one opens on a gloomy autumn evening in 1676 at Greville Cross in Lancashire.

The house was once a Benedictine monastery, granted at the Reformation to Sir Ralph de Greville. Its chapel and refectory lie ruined, and the family seldom visits. Readers get a historical tale of court life set in a bleak former monastery full of legend. Storm weather over the Lancashire coast opens the tale's first scene.
thomas-carlyle:
John Nichol, of Balliol College, Oxford, wrote a life of Thomas Carlyle dated 1904. His first note says the book rests on fresh study of Carlyle's work, slight first-hand views, and past lives of him. Froude, Carlyle's chosen literary legatee, stands as the chief source.

Nichol defends Froude against fierce, lasting attacks for printing too much about his hero. He notes Froude acted with explicit authority over the Reminiscences and memorials. Readers get a life that weighs Carlyle's gifts while asking how much a life writer may show, with Byron and Scott brought in for scale.
tom-swift-and-his-electric-rifle-or-dari:
Victor Appleton opens his elephant-land adventure with Tom Swift pausing at Ned's window in the Shopton National Bank. Tom asks whether Ned has anything special to do that night, and the bank clerk stacks bundles of bills while answering no. Contents promise twenty-five chapters of invention and hunting.

Headings move from trying the new gun through rush work to Africa by airship, a whale attack, an elephant stampede, and lions in the night. Missionaries need rescue, red pygmies are reported, and a rogue elephant closes the tale. Readers get a boys' adventure joining an electric rifle to an African expedition.
un-un-res-seventh-progress-report-of-the:
Mid-1999 in Sierra Leone is the span of the seventh progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1999/836. Talks at Lomé had just produced a peace deal between the government and the rebel front. The observer mission, UNOMSIL, now had to help turn paper promises into fact.

The report covers the deal's terms, plans for disarming fighters, and the return of people who had fled the war. It also notes deep distrust on all sides. The text captures a hopeful but fragile pause in a brutal war.
ungava-bob-a-winter-s-tale: Dillon Wallace wrote Ungava Bob, a winter's tale for boys. Grosset and Dunlap issued it at New York in 1907, in the Every Boy's Library Boy Scout edition, with pictures by Samuel M. Palmer. Wallace had earlier written The Lure of the Labrador Wild. The pages here give the title page and the start of the contents only, so the story itself is not shown. The first chapters promise how Bob got his trail, a start off to the bush, and an adventure with a bear.
vathek-an-arabian-tale:
William Beckford wrote Vathek, an Arabian tale first famous in French. This London edition of 1849, from George Slater, adds critical and explanatory notes. A memoir by William North opens the book. North gives Beckford's dates as 1760 to the spring of 1844. He regrets that so odd a man left no account of his own life. Beckford spent that life in learned retirement and strange pursuits.

North calls Vathek a bright ornament to French letters. Even Chateaubriand's Atala, he says, may not outlive it in French memory. He wishes all men of genius wrote their own lives, since such books teach later ages much. For Beckford, the facts are scant and hard to gather. Readers get the tale of the caliph Vathek with a life of its author in front, sketched from the few striking facts that survive.
victory-an-island-tale: Joseph Conrad wrote Victory: An Island Tale. Pages present here hold a Project Gutenberg title line and a bare contents list, so the novel itself is not shown. The contents name a note to the first edition and an author's note. Three parts follow, of seven or eight chapters each, with no chapter titles given. Nothing in these pages names the island, the hero, or the villains who reach him there. Readers learn only the book's frame: a late Conrad novel in three parts.
w-a-g-s-tale: Margaret Turnbull edited W.A.G.'s Tale, a child's story told in the first person. The title page credits its Zobzee illustrations to the author. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and a list of pictures only, so the tale itself is not shown. Nine chapters promise Uncle Burt's billy goat, the family house, and a next-door neighbor. Days on the towpath and on the Delaware, a boy named George, and a spell left alone follow. A white tent closes the list.
westways-a-village-chronicle:
S. Weir Mitchell published Westways, subtitled A Village Chronicle, in 1913. Mitchell gave the book to the memory of his three brothers, who all served in the Union armies. The tale centers on the Penhallow family and their village. Scenes from the Civil War stand behind the story.

Chapter one traces the first Penhallow, who crossed the Allegheny range before the war for independence. Later men of the family went to sea, to the army, or west. One James Penhallow grew rich in the China trade and came back home. Readers follow an old family line as war nears their quiet town.
what-led-to-the-discovery-of-the-source-: John Hanning Speke's short history of his first African journeys is represented here by its opening note alone, so the narrative itself is absent. Speke, a captain in the Indian Army, printed the book with Blackwood in 1864. He gave it to the memory of Sir James Outram, who first gave him a start in Africa. Friends urged him, he says, to tell what led to the Nile discovery. Parts first ran in Blackwood's Magazine. He links them to his solo trip to the Victoria N'yanza.
who-wrote-the-bible-a-book-for-the-peopl:
Washington Gladden wrote Who Wrote the Bible?, subtitled a book for the people. His contents run from a look into the Hebrew Bible to the worth of the whole book. Gladden says his aim is to give, in short and plain form, the main facts scholars agree on about how the Bible was written. Doctrine is not his topic here.

The human side of the book fills his pages: writing, copying, editing, keeping, and translating the texts. Gladden grants that the Bible holds more than human force. Yet its natural history, he argues, is the part most often skipped. Readers get a calm guide to Moses, the prophets, the Gospels, and the canon.
windsor-castle: The record here gives the title pages and a bare contents start for William Harrison Ainsworth's Windsor Castle, with no tale text shown. A line in the record dates the novel to 1843. Two quotes from Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor head the book, both on Herne the hunter and his midnight walks. The contents name book one as Anne Boleyn. Its chapters are numbered only, at least through nine. A twin record in the set carries the same front pages and goes on into the first chapter.
with-zola-in-england-a-story-of-exile: Ernest Alfred Vizetelly told this story of Emile Zola's exile in England. Pages present here hold a loving dedication to his wife and daughters, plus a long poem dated February 23, 1898. The poem pictures Zola begging for light, truth, and justice, and meeting darkness, falsehood, and threat instead. No prose chapters appear in these pages, so the exile story itself stays untold here.
wolfville:
Alfred Henry Lewis wrote these Western tales about a town called Wolfville. His preface says the stories come from an Old Cattleman narrator. Friends urged him to describe the town and its people in detail. Lewis refused. He left the town to Frederic Remington's pictures and to each reader's imagination instead.

The chapter list promises funerals, dance halls, elections, and foundlings. Recurring figures include Old Man Enright, Doc Peets, Cherokee Hall, and Faro Nell. Each tale stands as a barroom-style yarn. Readers get rough humour, loyalty, and sudden violence in a cow town setting.
writing-for-vaudeville:
Brett Page wrote this guide to writing vaudeville acts, with nine full example acts included. His foreword asks whether the skill can be taught at all. Talent matters, he says, yet craft and examples help. Page built the volume from magazine articles and months of gathering advice. Performers and writers across the trade helped him freely.

The example acts come from Richard Harding Davis, Aaron Hoffman, Edgar Allan Woolf, and others. Songs, sketches, and monologues all get treated. Page calls the volume the first treatise on its subject. Aspiring writers get forms, timing advice, and models to study.
wyandotte-or-the-hutted-knoll-a-tale:
J. Fenimore Cooper wrote this tale of an isolated family during colonial warfare, shown in an 1871 edition. His preface warns that border history is full of suffering legends. Cooper also scolds one-sided praise of the American Revolution. The cause had evil aspects too, he writes. Demagogues misled people in 1776, just as they do in his own day.

True patriotism, Cooper argues, must stay strictly just. That sober frame shapes the tale of the Hutted Knoll household. Readers get frontier danger mixed with hard questions about loyalty and blame. Neither side escapes fault in Cooper's telling.
